title: Baseline water quality and geochemistry of shallow groundwater used by indigenous communities in the vicinity of the Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Hannah Wudke, Gordon D.Z. Williams, Avner Vengosh
abstract: One of the largest global known lithium brine resources is the Salar de Uyuni (SDU) in the Bolivian Altiplano, yet presently, lithium exploitation is limited. Large-scale lithium extraction could impact regional water resources, which are used by local indigenous communities. Here, we investigate the water quality and geochemistry of shallow groundwater in the vicinity of the SDU, evaluating geochemical factors that control the occurrence of geogenic contaminants. We present a suite of geochemical analyses of shallow groundwater (n = 63) used as a primarily drinking water source by communities surrounding the SDU. Integrated water quality data shows that concentrations levels in most groundwater exceeded the World Health Organization drinking water recommended threshold values for at least one contaminant. We show that salinity, arsenic, boron and lithium are the major geogenic constituents that pose risks to human health. These results are consistent with established patterns of geogenic water quality issues reported for other water resources in the high Andes. Our analysis shows that low salinity groundwater west of the SDU is characterized by low δ2H and δ18O with a slope that mimics the Local Meteoric Water Line and distinctively high boron, B/Li, Mg/Li, and low 87Sr/86Sr, indicating water-rock interactions with associated andesitic rocks. Groundwater from the Rio Grande watershed and eastern of the SDU have higher δ2H, δ18O, and 87Sr/86Sr, reflecting local recharge and different lithological sources with a radiogenic Sr isotope composition. Through the region we identified hot spots of saline groundwater with low B/Li and Mg/Li ratios and with relatively low δ2H and δ18O, as well as 87Sr/86Sr ratios that are different from those of the SDU brines, indicating rather mixing with underlying saline geothermal waters. Future large-scale lithium extraction could intensify groundwater pumping that would be likely to cause regional groundwater level drawdown and further increase the impact of underlying saline geothermal waters, exacerbating the already impaired quality of water resources for indigenous communities in the SDU vicinity.

title: Spatial distribution of mercury in sediment from coastal environments around Cuba
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Yoelvis Bolaños-Alvarez, Ana Carolina Ruiz-Fernández, Misael Díaz-Asencio, Yusmila Helguera Pedraza, Oscar Díaz-Rizo, Gustavo Arencibia-Carballo, Miguel Gómez-Batista, Joan-Albert Sanchez-Cabeza, Vanessa Hatje, Carlos M. Alonso-Hernández
abstract: Mercury (Hg) contamination in coastal sediments poses significant ecological and health risks, necessitating comprehensive assessments under the Minamata Convention. This study investigates the spatial distribution and potential ecological risks of Hg in surface sediments from 15 diverse Cuban coastal environments. Sediment samples were collected and analyzed for total Hg (ranging from 0.001 to 16.5 mg kg−1), and a reference value of 0.090 ± 0.059 mg kg−1, defined as the geochemical background level for Hg in marine sediments, was derived using a cumulative distribution function method. Contamination degree was assessed using the Contamination Factor (CF) and the ecological risk was quantified using the Ecological Risk Index, the Threshold Effect Level (TEL), the Probable Effect Level (PEL), and the novel Composite Environmental Vulnerability Index (CEVI). Results revealed pronounced Hg enrichment in anthropogenically influenced sites, with Sagua la Grande River and Havana Bay exhibiting extremely high CF values and frequent exceedances of the PEL, identifying them as regional hotspots driven by industrial legacies and urban pressures. The CEVI effectively linked Hg levels to industrial and population factors. Compared to global hotspots, these findings provide a critical baseline for Cuba, supporting Minamata Convention monitoring and urging future studies to focus on temporal data, speciation, and bioaccumulation.

title: Genesis of the uraniferous black slates in the Biryeri deposit of the Ogcheon Metamorphic Belt, South Korea: Mineralogy, geochemistry, fluid inclusion and stable isotope
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Jinah Lim, Dongbok Shin, Jaeguk Jo, Heonkyung Im, Ji-Hun Ryu
abstract: Uraniferous black slates of the Biryeri deposit in the Ogcheon Metamorphic Belt (OMB), South Korea, record multistage uranium enrichment within a rift-related black shale system subsequently modified by hydrothermal activity and regional metamorphism. This study integrates mineralogical, whole-rock geochemical, fluid inclusion, Raman spectroscopic, and stable isotope (C–O–H–S) data to constrain the origin and evolution of mineralization in black slate and interbedded coaly slate. The two lithologies exhibit contrasting mineral assemblages. Black slate contains mainly coffinite and brannerite, whereas the coaly slate is dominated by uraninite associated with quartz veins, V-rich muscovite, goldmanite, molybdenite, and Ni-bearing sulfides. The coaly slate is strongly enriched in U (up to 1651 ppm), V, Mo, and Ni and shows Mn depletion. High V/Cr and V/(V + Ni) ratios, elevated U and Mo enrichment factors, positive Eu anomalies, and high U/Th and Nd/Yb ratios indicate modification by high-temperature (>250 °C) hydrothermal fluids under strongly reducing conditions. Fluid inclusions temperatures of 253–450 °C and isotope data are consistent with the magmatic water range, with limited seawater or meteoric input. Carbon and sulfur isotopes indicate a marine black shale precursor subsequently overprinted by thermochemical sulfate reduction. Uranium mineralization at the Biryeri deposit reflects a multi-stage evolution involving black shale sedimentation in a rift-related marine basin, magmatic–hydrothermal remobilization and upgrading, and low-grade metamorphic recrystallization, highlighting the key role of magmatic fluids in concentrating uranium within black shale system under reducing environments.

title: Dissolution and surface chemical modifications of mineral fibres in artificial lysosomal fluid
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Maria Cristina Di Carlo, Paolo Ballirano, Lorenzo Arrizza, Maria Rita Montereali, Marzia Fantauzzi, Antonella Rossi, Giancarlo Capitani, Niccolò Magnani, Marcello Campione, Rossella Yivlialin, Gianlorenzo Bussetti, Antonella Campopiano, Annapaola Cannizzaro, Andrea Bloise, Fabrizio Bardelli, Ida Pettiti, Alessandro Pacella
abstract: The long-term toxicity of mineral fibres is closely related to their biodurability and surface reactivity, which are in turn strongly influenced by mineral dissolution and surface alteration in lung fluids. We investigated dissolution rates and nanoscale structural, morphological and surface chemical modifications of fibrous antigorite, a non-regulated serpentine polymorph of uncertain pathogenicity, amphibole asbestos (crocidolite and tremolite) and chrysotile, after incubation in artificial lysosomal fluid at pH 4.5, simulating the acidic environment of alveolar macrophages. Fibres were incubated at 37 °C for up to 4 weeks; elemental release was quantified by ICP-OES, and recovered fibres were characterized by PXRD, XPS, FE-SEM, AFM, and TEM. All fibres dissolved incongruently, with preferential leaching of octahedrally coordinated cations and Fe mobilization promoted by citrate complexation. Chrysotile dissolved extensively and became progressively amorphous, consistent with its high specific surface area and preferential removal of Mg from outer octahedral layers. When Si-based dissolution rates are normalised to specific surface area, fibrous antigorite displays biodurability comparable to chrysotile and at least one order of magnitude lower than amphibole asbestos. Among amphiboles, tremolite dissolves more slowly than crocidolite, for which surface erosion exposes underlying Fe(II)-rich layers. Despite the simplified, acellular nature of the ALF model, our results show trends in incongruent dissolution, Fe mobilisation and surface amorphization consistent with in vivo toxicological observations. Integration of ALF-based mineralogical and geochemical data with targeted cellular and in vivo studies may provide a more robust mechanistic framework for understanding the long-term toxicity of both asbestos and currently unregulated fibrous minerals.

title: Hydrological controls on carbon isotope signal transfer and kinetic overprinting in a subtropical karst system, Southwest China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Xia Wu, Moucheng Pan, Jianjun Yin, Jianhua Cao
abstract: Interpreting speleothem carbon isotope (δ13C) records as paleohydrological proxies necessitates a mechanistic understanding of signal transfer within the karst critical zone. This study presents a high-resolution monitoring program (2023–2025) encompassing soil CO2, drip water, and modern carbonate precipitates in Liangfeng Cave, southwest China, specifically assessing the impact of seasonal hydrological extremes. Seasonal variations in soil CO2 concentration and δ13CCO2 broadly corresponded with changes in drip water δ13CDIC, while HCO3 − and δ13CDIC exhibited a negative relationship across the monitored sites, consistent with an important contribution from seasonally varying biogenic carbon inputs. However, the transmission of this primary environmental signal exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity, modulated by local hydrogeological routing and microclimatic gradients. At proximal, well-ventilated sites, reduced drip rates during hydrological deficits prolong fluid residence times, potentially promoting kinetic 13C enrichment and prior calcite precipitation (PCP), which may contribute to the apparent decoupling of the DIC–carbonate isotopic offset from the seasonal temperature gradient. Conversely, distal, deep-cave sites with stable microclimates appear to show reduced sensitivity to short-term hydrological forcing at the temporal resolution of this study, maintaining a relatively stable isotopic regime. Furthermore, extreme hydrological deficits are associated with pronounced departures from the typical seasonal isotopic pattern, generating substantial positive δ13C anomalies that may reflect kinetic overprinting and complicate their direct interpretation as indicators of aridity. These findings highlight the need to evaluate site-specific kinetic effects in similar shallow or well-ventilated cave settings before paleoclimatic interpretation.

title: Kinetics of CO 2 degassing and carbonate mineral precipitation from thermal waters: the Bollore springs in Bagni San Filippo (Italy)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Giuseppe D. Saldi, Maximiliano Fastelli, Vasileios Mavromatis, Jean-Michel Brazier, Francesco Frondini
abstract: CO2 outgassing from thermal springs represents an efficient transfer process of deep geogenic gas to the atmosphere. At Bollore, in the Bagni San Filippo area (Siena province, Tuscany), the rapid CO2 release by hydrothermal springs emerging at 44-49 °C is accompanied by the formation of abundant carbonate deposits. Simultaneous sampling of precipitates and water flowing through a series of pools downstream of the main spring emergence allowed for estimates of carbonate precipitation rates, local CO2 fluxes and the contribution of groundwater discharge to the regional CO2 budget. Obtained results suggest that the total CO2 exsolved from flowing waters (2.6-4.5 × 106 mol/yr) is 4-7 times higher than sequestered in precipitated carbonates (0.4-1.3 × 106 mol/yr). Aragonite is the dominant phase precipitating from the hydrothermal waters, favored by the relatively high temperatures, the high pCO2 (0.1-2.5 bar) and Mg/Ca aqueous ratio, as well as the abundant aqueous SO4 2−. Analyses of various trace elements in both the thermal waters and the precipitated solids allowed calculations of the partition coefficients showing preferential uptake of Ba and Sr, which is generally consistent with aragonite formation. Calculated aragonite precipitation rates, even though affected by high uncertainties, result ∼4 to 30 times faster compared to the rates derived from experimental data. The CO2 released by the Bollore-Bagni San Filippo hydrothermal waters is significant at the local scale (∼1580 t/yr) but appears negligible when compared with the regional fluxes from soil diffuse degassing (∼0.5% of total CO2 release). Therefore, travertine deposition and direct gas release through groundwater discharge represent only a small fraction of the total regional CO2 flux but remain a significant component of deep CO2 degassing. Taking these contributions into account complements soil diffuse degassing surveys, allowing for more accurate estimates of regional CO2 budgets.

title: Hydrogeochemical constraints on an intracrustal magma-driven and fault controlled high-temperature geothermal system (Daggyai) in southern Tibet
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Bin Wang, Mingliang Liu, Hongjie Shi, Xianbin Zhu, Meihua Wei, Gaojing Ren, Qinghai Guo
abstract: High-temperature geothermal systems in southern Tibet are commonly associated with crustal magmatism and active faulting, but how magmatic heat, fault-controlled circulation, and shallow fluid processes jointly shape their surface hydrochemical signatures remains poorly constrained. Here, we investigate the Daggyai geothermal field on the northern margin of the Yarlung Zangbo Suture Zone using a field-derived dataset of 27 geothermal water samples. In situ physicochemical measurements, major and trace element concentrations, and δD and δ18O compositions were integrated with field structural observations, mineral–fluid equilibrium assessment, geothermometry, Cl-based binary mixing calculations, and isotope reconstruction. The waters comprise 22 alkaline samples (Group 1), three acidic samples (Group 2), and two weakly acidic mixed-type samples (Group 3). Group 1 waters are enriched in Cl, B, Li, and As and preserve the clearest signatures of deep reservoir fluids. Group 2 waters are interpreted as steam-heated waters formed through the condensation and oxidation of H2S-bearing vapor in shallow groundwater, whereas Group 3 records mixing between deep and shallow fluid components. Mineral–fluid equilibrium relationships and Na–K geothermometry indicate a deep reservoir temperature of 252.6–262.5 °C. Reconstructed deep-fluid isotope compositions exhibit pronounced 18O enrichment relative to local meteoric water, consistent with high-temperature water–rock interaction and a magmatic-fluid contribution. These results support a process-based model in which intracrustal magmatic heat sustains the high-temperature reservoir, while deep faults govern meteoric recharge and geothermal-fluid ascent; boiling and near-surface mixing subsequently generate the observed hydrochemical diversity. This study distinguishes deep magmatic and structural controls from shallow geochemical overprinting and provides a transferable framework for the genetic interpretation and resource evaluation of high-temperature geothermal systems in southern Tibet.

title: Size-resolved characterization of iron nanoparticles in Tibetan Plateau glacier meltwater using SP-ICP-MS
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Hongmei An, Shaopeng Gao, Xin Wan, David Widory, Xing Diao, Chunhui Wang, Zhiyong Zhu, Qianggong Zhang, Zhiyuan Cong
abstract: Iron nanoparticles (FeNPs) are an important but analytically challenging component of iron in glacier meltwater due to their low concentrations, high particulate loads, and strong dissolved iron backgrounds. Here, we optimized and validated a single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (SP-ICP-MS) method for the size-resolved characterization and quantification of FeNPs in glacier meltwater. By integrating SP-ICP-MS measurements with conventional operational definitions of iron fractions, the <0.45 μm dissolved iron pool is partitioned into nanoparticle iron and baseline dissolved iron. Additionally, when the dissolved Fe background is < 0.37 ng mL−1, it provides a coherent framework compatible with established glacial geochemical datasets. Method evaluation demonstrates that both the filtration strategy and dissolved iron background exert first order controls on the detection of FeNPs. Results show that the 0.45 μm filtration offers the most robust balance between removing coarse-particle interference and retaining representative FeNPs populations. In contrast, finer filtration leads to their systematic underestimation, whereas not filtering samples elevates and distorts particle pulse intensities and inflates SP-ICP-MS-derived particle sizes. The application of the proposed optimized method to meltwaters from the Tibetan Plateau's Kuoqionggangri and Rongbuk glacier systems reveals a consistent iron partitioning scheme, with particulate iron dominating total iron and FeNPs constituting a persistent but quantitatively subordinate fraction of the <0.45 μm pool. Despite variability in iron concentrations and hydrological settings, FeNPs exhibit stable modal particle diameters within the 19.6 to 46.8 nm range, indicating a reproducible nanometer-scale signature of glacially derived iron. Overall, this study establishes SP-ICP-MS as a robust and operationally constrained method for resolving iron nanoparticles in glacier meltwater and provides a practical basis for consistent size-resolved investigations of iron in cryospheric environments.

title: Li and REE geochemical behaviour during mineral precipitation in hyperalkaline soda brines: insights from the Rincón de Parangueo Maar (Mexico)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Claudio Inguaggiato, Sabrina Pappaterra, Gilles Levresse, Loïc Peiffer, Dmitri Rouwet, Carmine Apollaro, Benedetto Schiavo, Lorenzo Brusca
abstract: This study focuses on the geochemistry of Rare Earth Elements (REE) and Li in the hyperalkaline soda brine of the remnant Rincón de Parangueo (RDP) maar lake, Mexico, a system characterized by the ongoing precipitation of trona, thermonatrite, halite and sylvite. Total REE concentrations in water range between 13.5 and 26.9 μg kg−1, while higher concentrations (688-1302 μg kg−1) were found in the associated bulk mineral precipitates (trona, thermonatrite, halite and sylvite). Lithium concentrations are higher than REE concentrations, in both RDP waters and bulk minerals. Lithium concentrations in RDP waters and bulk minerals precipitated are quite similar, ranging from 53.8 to 126.5 mg kg−1 and from 51.3 to 149.1 mg kg−1, respectively. Post Archean Australian shale (PAAS) normalized REE patterns in the waters increase from La to Lu. In contrast, PAAS normalized REE patterns of the bulk minerals are different from those of waters, also increasing from La to Lu but with a less pronounced trend. The distribution coefficient (KD) of REE and Li were calculated between the bulk precipitated minerals and the coexisting lake water. KD values of REE decrease from La to Lu and are significantly higher (6-1154), compared to KD values of Li (0.5-0.8). The REE patterns in waters, which increase from La to Lu, can be explained by the KD values, indicating preferential removal of LREE relative to HREE during mineral precipitation. Similar lithium concentration ranges in waters and bulk minerals are consistent with the low KD of Li, indicating a limited removal of Li from the solution during mineral precipitation.

title: High-temporal-resolution tracking of manganese(III/IV) (hydr)oxide dissolution kinetics induced by low-molecular-weight organic compounds
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Junhui Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xuesheng Xu, Jiayi Yao, Yingzhe Li, Zehao Zhou, Chuan Liu, Xulin Jiang, Yandi Hu, Kai Li, Dongqiang Zhu
abstract: The dissolution of manganese (Mn) (hydr)oxides induced by low-molecular-weight organic compounds (LMWOCs) critically influences Mn and carbon cycling, yet limited high-resolution characterization hinders mechanistic understanding. Here, we investigated the dissolution kinetics of Mn(III/IV) (hydr)oxides mediated by citric acid, pyruvic acid, oxalic acid, and hydroquinone, as well as the controlling factors (LMWOC type and concentration, pH, and coexisting ions), by real-time and in-situ electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM), complemented by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) and kinetic modeling. Hydroquinone and citric acid promoted significant dissolution at pH 5 and 6, with hydroquinone dominating initially but slowing later; at pH 7, hydroquinone remained highly effective, far surpassing citric acid. In contrast, pyruvic acid and oxalic acid at pH 5, 6, and 7 showed negligible dissolution. Citric acid– and hydroquinone–mediated dissolution exhibited characteristic S-shaped kinetics with induction, acceleration, and deceleration stages, indicating an autocatalytic pathway, whereas pyruvic acid and oxalic acid showed no such pattern. Analysis of controlling factors showed that citric acid–mediated dissolution increased with increasing citric acid concentration and decreasing pH. Coexisting ions, including NO3 −, Cl−, SO4 2− (5–50 mM), and Mg2+, Ca2+, Zn2+ (0.5–4 mM), inhibited the dissolution. Notably, HPO4 2− and P2O7 4− (0.1–1 mM) and Mn2+ (0.5–4 mM) exhibited concentration-dependent dual effects on dissolution, arising from competing promotive and inhibitory processes. GIWAXS analysis revealed that citric acid–mediated dissolution of Mn(III/IV) (hydr)oxides was facet-dependent, whereas exogenous Mn2+ promoted non-selective citric acid–mediated dissolution. This study provides insights into complex interfacial geochemical processes on redox-active minerals.

title: Application of a luminescence-based oxygen measuring system for quantifying dissolved O 2 consumption by Fe(II)-bearing geologic media
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Mitsuo Manaka, Mikio Takeda
abstract: Fe(II)-bearing geologic media are a promising sink for the consumption of dissolved oxygen (DO) remaining in geologic formations after backfilling of radioactive waste repositories, which prevents redox-sensitive radionuclides from becoming soluble and mobile in groundwater. To assess the effect of DO, the DO consumption rate has been measured using commercially available oxygen electrodes and electrochemical techniques; however, when performing DO consumption experiments in closed systems with respect to DO, DO consumption associated with electrochemical measurements, independent of water–rock interactions, remains an issue that requires improvement. To address this, we propose a measurement system for quantifying DO consumption. Accordingly, DO consumption experiments on Fe(II)-bearing rock samples were performed using a luminescence-based oxygen sensor without oxygen consumption. The samples used in this study were selected as sedimentary samples that had been previously investigated, because the applicability of the sensor was evaluated, as well as the addition of the rate data. Consequently, the DO concentration in the experimental solution decreased as previously observed. However, this decrease in DO can be primarily attributed to the consumption of DO by Fe(II)-bearing minerals in the rock samples, rather than interference from the oxygen sensor. The resulting second-order rate constants strongly support the previously reported rate data and improve reproducibility for this measurement system. These findings contribute to preliminary predictions of recovery from oxic to anoxic conditions in geologic formations and provide insight into the temporal evolution of subsurface DO in the vicinity of a repository.

title: Intrinsic alkalinity of the reactive media regulates the differential immobilization of As(V) and Sb(V) in co-contaminated groundwater
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Wen Zhang, Kai-hua Bai, Jun Tang, Yi-long Zhao, Jun Jiang
abstract: The simultaneous immobilization of arsenic (As) and antimony (Sb) in groundwater is challenged by their competitive interactions, which are strongly influenced by pH fluctuations and complex speciation. Based on permeable reactive barrier (PRB) technology, this study demonstrates the feasibility of manipulating the intrinsic alkalinity of goethite-based fillers using cement to effectively immobilize As(V) and Sb(V) in co-contaminated groundwater. Ordinary Portland cement (OPC), slag-modified Portland cement (SPC), and sulphoaluminate cement (SAC) with distinct hydration reaction were used as binders to fabricate goethite-based fillers with varying solid-phase alkalinity gradients. Batch experiments revealed that the OPC-filler with the highest alkalinity demonstrated preferable immobilization capacity for both As(V) and Sb(V) compared with the SPC- and SAC-fillers under varying initial pH, coexisting ions, and natural organic matter conditions. Duration tests confirmed that the OPC-filler could maintain stable immobilization of both As (>98%) and Sb (>86%) under high-flow-rate accelerated conditions, whereas the other fillers showed rapid Sb breakthrough. Integrated post-test characterizations and geochemical modeling revealed a dual immobilization pathway in the filler: As(V) was primarily immobilized via adsorption onto goethite, whereas Sb(V) immobilization was enhanced by the high-alkalinity microenvironment, which promoted the precipitation of calcium with Sb(V). These findings demonstrate that engineering the intrinsic solid-phase alkalinity of goethite-based PRB filler is an effective strategy for achieving simultaneous immobilization of As(V) and Sb(V) in groundwater.

title: Dynamics and drivers of CO 2 emissions in agricultural river-ditch networks: management and wetland degradation effects
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Xia Li, Xiao-Dong Li, Si-Liang Li, Shi-Yuan Ding, Wan-Fa Wang, Li Bai, Min Xiao, Ming-Guo Wang, Xiao-Long Liu
abstract: As a cornerstone of Northeast China's “grain basket,” the Sanjiang Plain hosts expansive irrigation and drainage networks that function as intensive biogeochemical reactors. However, their contribution to global carbon dioxide (CO2) budgets and mechanisms regulating CO2 production and emissions remains a major uncertainty. Therefore, this study examined the spatiotemporal variations of CO2 concentrations and emission fluxes (fCO2) in a representative wetland-river-ditch network in the Sanjiang Plain, Northeast China. Results revealed that most of the rivers and drainage ditches were highly supersaturated with CO2, acting as atmospheric sources. The fCO2 ranged from −20.7 to 288.9 mmol m−2 d−1 in rivers and reached up to 422.7 mmol m−2 d−1 in ditches, identifying ditches as distinct emission hotspots. Stoichiometric relationships (ΔCO2/ΔO2) and C/N ratios indicated that CO2 production was primarily associated with internal metabolic processes. Furthermore, wetland degradation and agricultural fertilization may enhance carbon export and microbial respiration, facilitating the emission of CO2. Overall, irrigation and drainage networks represent important components of agricultural carbon cycling and should be considered in regional carbon budget assessments and wetland management strategies.

title: Source of uranium (U) and rare earth elements (REE) for unconformity-related U and REE mineralization in the Athabasca Basin, Canada: Insights from accessory minerals in sandstones
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Goktug Harmanci, Guoxiang Chi, Jeremy Powell, Janina Czas, Victoria Tschirhart, Huimin Su, Yumeng Wang, Nahanni Danylczuk
abstract: The Athabasca Basin in Canada hosts the world's largest and highest-grade unconformity-related uranium (URU) deposits, many of which are also enriched in rare earth elements (REE). There has been a long-lasting debate whether the U and REE were sourced from the basin or basement. This study investigates the potential contribution of detrital accessory minerals in the basin, particularly zircon and Ti-oxide (rutile), to U and REE mineralization. The textural and compositional characteristics of these detrital accessory minerals, as well as diagenetic minerals, including Ti-oxide (anatase), iron oxide/hydroxide (IOH) and aluminium phosphate sulfate (APS) minerals, were examined using multiple in-situ analytical methods. The results show that detrital zircon and rutile exhibit extensive dissolution and alteration features and large and irregular variations of U and REE concentrations within individual grains suggesting strong fluid-rock interactions. Large amounts of U and REE, especially heavy REE (HREE), were leached into the basinal brines, while some of them, especially light REE (LREE), were retained by diagenetic minerals. The resulting diagenetic basinal fluids are characterized by strong HREE enrichment, which broadly match the REE patterns of uraninite in the URU ores. Mass balance calculations suggest that 40 to 70 million tonnes of U and 80 to 330 million tonnes of REE, depending on the methods of calculation, could be leached from zircon and rutile. Despite the large variations and uncertainties, these estimations far exceed the amounts found in the URU deposits, implying significant potentials for further U and REE exploration. The results also highlight the vulnerability of zircon and rutile to hydrothermal alteration under certain conditions in sedimentary basins and its significance for large-scale U and REE mineralization.

title: Rheological properties of sensitive marine clays stabilised by inorganic salts - impact of anion and cation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Kamila Zabłocka, Mohammad Hemayati, Rene Tammen, Erika Eiser, Seyed Ali Ghoreishian Amiri, Barbara Lothenbach, Harald Justnes, Priscilla Paniagua, Klaartje De Weerdt
abstract: This study investigates (1) the applicability of parallel plate rheology for assessing quick clay stabilisation by inorganic salts and (2) the short-term stabilising effects of selected cation–anion combinations. Quick clay from the Tiller-Flotten geotechnical test site was treated with salt solutions containing Na+, K+, Ca2+ and Mg2+ paired with Cl−, OH−, SO4 2− and CO3 2− at concentrations between 0.037 and 0.6 M. A dedicated rheometer protocol enabled extraction of dynamic and static yield shear strengths and structural build-up, revealing non-Newtonian shear-thinning behaviour. Dynamic yield strength from the upwards flow curve was used as the primary parameter and showed good correlation with falling-cone shear strength, with rheology offering higher precision, reproducibility, and reduced sample size. Increasing salt concentration consistently enhanced shear strength, with clear ion-specific trends. Divalent chlorides (CaCl2, MgCl2) were most effective at low concentrations but reached a plateau near 0.2 M, while monovalent chlorides continued to increase the strength, with KCl outperforming NaCl at higher concentrations due to the smaller hydration shell and stronger adsorption of K+. Anion effects were strongly governed by pH: Cl− and SO4 2− (neutral pH) promoted flocculation at low concentrations, whereas OH− and CO3 2− (high pH) required higher cation concentrations to counteract initial deflocculation. Ca(OH)2 produced the highest shear strength overall. The geotechnical stability criterion of 0.33 kPa was reached for all K-salts and for Ca(OH)2. Overall, the results show that short-term stabilisation of quick clay is controlled by cation valence, hydration radius, and anion-dependent pH, providing a mechanistic basis for designing more efficient binders for rapid ground improvement.

title: Integrated experimental and computational investigation of Rhodamine B adsorption onto Moroccan stevensite clay: Kinetics, isotherms, thermodynamics, DSD optimization, DFT, and Monte Carlo analysis
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Jaber Raissouni, El Houssain Chkouri, Ahmed Ait Aghzzaf, María J. Fernández-Sanjurjo, Avelino Núñez-Delgado, Esperanza Álvarez-Rodríguez, Khalid Draoui
abstract: The discharge of synthetic organic dyes into industrial wastewater constitutes a serious environmental problem due to the persistence, toxicity, and non-biodegradable nature of these pollutants. In this study, the adsorption removal of Rhodamine B (RhB), a toxic cationic dye, was investigated using natural stevensite-rich Ghassoul clay (SW) as an abundant, low-cost, and eco-friendly adsorbent. The clay was characterized using FTIR, SEM/EDS, XRD, XRF, and zeta potential analyses to determine its structural and physicochemical properties. Adsorption kinetics showed rapid RhB uptake followed by equilibrium after approximately 60 min, with an experimental adsorption capacity of 94.1 mg g−1 and 94.1% removal efficiency. The pseudo-second-order kinetic model provided the best fit (R2 ≈ 0.9996), suggesting that adsorption was controlled mainly by surface interactions and diffusion processes. Equilibrium data were analyzed using several nonlinear isotherm models. Heterogeneous models, particularly Fritz–Schluender V, Redlich–Peterson, and Sips, produced the best statistical fits (R2 ≈ 0.996), indicating adsorption on energetically heterogeneous surfaces through combined monolayer, multilayer, and pore-filling mechanisms. The nonlinear Langmuir model predicted a maximum adsorption capacity of 208.85 mg g−1. Thermodynamic analysis confirmed that adsorption was spontaneous and endothermic. The Definitive Screening Design (DSD) approach optimized operational parameters influencing adsorption performance. Complementary Density Functional Theory (DFT), topological analyses using the program Multiwfn, and Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, and π–π interactions govern RhB adsorption onto stevensite surfaces.

title: Chromium mica geochemistry as a potential indicator of Au mineralization: Evidence from the Dongcaogou and Haopinggou Au deposits, Eastern Qinling, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Hu Ziqi, Zhang Dexian, Xiao Dian, Zhou Jialing, He Hao
abstract: Chromium mica (fuchsite) alteration is widely developed in gold (Au) deposits across the Western Qinling and Xiong'ershan districts, yet its specific relationship with Au mineralization remains poorly constrained. This study systematically investigates the structural characteristics, major and trace element compositions, and fluid-mineral relationships of chromium mica from the Dongcaogou and Haopinggou polymetallic deposits, Eastern Qinling, China. Analytical results demonstrate systematic spatial variations in unit-cell parameters and geochemical signatures: chromium mica from shallow-level Dongcaogou display expanded cell volumes (918-941 Å3) with elevated Cr2O3 (0.01-10.07%) and K2O (3.17-6.97%), indicative of intensive alteration linked to gold enrichment, whereas deep-seated Haopinggou samples exhibit smaller cell volumes (915 Å3) of phengitic composition, reflecting high-pressure, low-strain conditions. Elemental correlations (Cr-Al-K-Fe-Zn) reveal metal-enrichment processes in ore-forming fluids, with increasing Cr content signaling key mineralization drivers including reduced oxygen fugacity, acidic pH, and intense fluid-rock interaction. These findings establish chromium mica as a valuable exploration indicator for Au mineralization in the Eastern Qinling orogenic belt.

title: Paleoclimate imprint and recharge conditions of the northwestern Caucasus groundwater: an isotopic study of the Azov-Kuban Artesian Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Igor Tokarev, Evgeny Yakovlev, Tatiana Lyubimova, Andrey Puchkov, Sergey Druzhinin, Roman Smagin, Valeriya Timoshina, Alexey Tudvachev, Artem Konkin
abstract: The article investigates the isotopic characteristics and origin of groundwater within the Quaternary and Neogene aquifers of the Azov-Kuban Artesian Basin (AKAB), Northwestern Caucasus. Isotopic analysis revealed the presence of a distinct “Late Pleistocene fossil groundwater” water component in the deeper sedimentary horizons. These groundwaters are significantly depleted in heavy isotopes, with δ18O values ranging from −17.54‰ to −12.50‰ (mean −14.76‰) and δ2H from −146.1‰ to −89.0‰ (mean −107.4‰). The total absence of tritium and radiocarbon dating results (26-34 ka) confirm that these resources are paleowaters. In contrast, modern groundwater in the recharge areas of the AKAB foothills (200-400 m a.s.l.) exhibits enriched isotopic signatures, with mean values of −10.81‰ for δ18O and −75.5‰ for δ2H. These signatures closely match the weighted mean isotopic composition of local precipitation during the recharge season (−10.7‰ for δ18O and −73.8‰ for δ2H). The presence of tritium and anthropogenic nitrate pollution in the upper geological section further validates the modern origin of these waters. A comparison between the recharge waters and the deep-seated “Late Pleistocene fossil groundwater” component indicates that the latter originated during the cold climatic stage of the Late Pleistocene. The spatial distribution of δ18O and δ2H shows that the proportion of paleowater increases with depth and distance from the foothill recharge zones. These findings provide essential evidence of paleoclimatic imprints on the regional hydrogeological system, highlighting the vulnerability of fossil groundwater reserves.

title: Strontium isotopic evidence for heterogeneous sediment-water interactions in inland groundwater of the western Bengal Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Pousali Pathak, Deependra Singh, Vineet Goswami, Prosenjit Ghosh
abstract: Evaluation of relative contributions of aquifer bulk mineral sources on groundwater chemistry remains challenging owing to heterogeneous hydrostratigraphy and seasonally variable hydrogeochemistry. The diverse geochemical composition of Ganga-Brahmaputra floodplain sediments found in inland aquifers of the Bengal Basin, and their impact on groundwater chemistry over seasonal timescales, are not well understood. This study combines seasonal groundwater geochemistry with isotope-based mass-balance modeling to constrain the controls on dissolved Sr and 87Sr/86Sr in depth-bound inland groundwater from the western Bengal Basin, India, located within the Hooghly/Ganga floodplain. To understand the spatial variations in inland groundwater compositions across the Bengal floodplain, the present database has been compared with available data from the eastern Bengal Basin (Bangladesh) located in both the Ganga and Brahmaputra drainage basins. Shallow groundwater exhibits variable hydrogeochemistry and Ca/Sr molar ratios together with relatively radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr that show limited seasonal variability, whereas dissolved solute concentrations are generally higher during the pre-monsoon period. By Comparison with available geochemical data for Ganga River bedload sediment-water, we suggest that (i) detrital carbonate dissolution accounts for an estimated 74-93% of Sr release to shallow groundwater, and (ii) localized silicate weathering contributes to heterogeneous Sr release with radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr in seasonal shallow groundwater, followed by secondary interactions with exchangeable clay-sediment fractions. Secondary interactions with exchangeable clay-sediment fractions may subsequently modify dissolved Sr concentrations and Ca/Sr ratios without substantially influencing 87Sr/86Sr. Further, we estimate that inland groundwater discharge from the western Bengal Basin delivers (8.8 ± 3.9) × 105 mol yr−1 of Sr to the Hooghly/Ganga River.

title: Germanium and its isotopes in saline and brine groundwaters (Western Carpathians, Poland): Effects of diagenetic processes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Dariusz Dobrzyński, Marek Duliński, Jakub Karasiński, Klaudia Tetfejer, Andrii Tupys, Marcin Stępień, Katarzyna Wątor, Lucyna Rajchel
abstract: The germanium (Ge) content and its isotope ratio (IR) in saline and brine groundwaters from the Polish Outer Carpathians and Carpathian Foredeep (southern Poland) have been investigated. The Ge IR of continental groundwater in such geological environments has not previously been studied. This study found a wide variation in Ge concentrations in the groundwaters, increasing in the order of the following chemical water types: Na-Cl brines (<0.5–2.6 μg/L), Na-Cl saline waters (<0.5–42 μg/L), and Na-HCO3 saline waters (1.1–104 μg/L). The variation in Ge concentration is due to the different formation histories of the current composition of each water, including the mixing of formation water with infiltration water. The germanium in the studied formation water is derived mainly from minerals and organic matter transformed during the diagenesis of rock formations. The mixing of formation water with infiltration water results in a lower Ge concentration. In the Na-HCO3 saline groundwater, elevated Ge concentrations are accompanied by isotopically heavier oxygen compositions (with δ18O values of up to 6.2‰) due to the presence of dehydration water, which is released during the transformation of clay minerals, mainly the illitisation of smectite. The Ge IR values, which span a wide range (δ74/70Ge from 0.97‰ to 5.21‰), exceed previously reported values for continental groundwaters (1.21‰–4.02‰; Siebert et al., 2006; Baronas et al., 2020; Dobrzyński et al., 2024) and show greater enrichment in isotopically heavy Ge than continental crustal rocks (average δ74/70Ge value of 0.58 ± 0.21‰). The enrichment of the studied waters in heavier Ge isotopes was plausibly caused by the preferential removal of light isotopes by iron oxyhydroxides and clay minerals. The Ge IR values of formation waters are changed by (1) possible mixing with infiltration water components and, in the case of the shallowest water intakes, (2) the preferential immobilization of light Ge isotopes by secondary Fe oxyhydroxides and clay minerals abundantly present in the near-surface zone.

title: Investigating iron–sulphur–phosphate transformation dynamics during redox-controlled microaeration of digested sludge towards improved resource recovery
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Sophie Banke, Femke Deelstra, Thomas Prot, Leon Korving, Carlo Belloni, Iulian A. Dugulan, Mark C.M. van Loosdrecht
abstract: Iron is an attractive binding partner for phosphorus removal from digested sludge, with recovery as the Fe(II) phosphate mineral vivianite (Fe3(PO4)2·8H2O) representing a promising resource recovery pathway. However, sulphides compete strongly with phosphate for Fe(II), limiting vivianite formation and often requiring higher iron dosages. Because both iron and sulphur undergo redox transformations, controlled microaeration may alter the balance between iron sulphides, iron phosphates, and oxidized iron and sulphur species. This study investigated the effect of oxidation–reduction potential (ORP)-controlled microaeration (−220 to 0 mV) on Fe–S–P transformations in digested sludge. Microaeration showed contrasting effects. Mössbauer spectroscopy indicated an approximately 20% decrease in the Fe(II) associated with the vivianite fraction under all ORP conditions, while a pyrite-like iron sulphide phase remained largely unchanged. In contrast, the soluble phase showed increasing sulphur concentrations (ultimately recovered as sulphate) and a ∼70% decrease in soluble phosphorus, suggesting enhanced iron–phosphate binding or adsorption during microaeration. Although the applied aeration conditions ultimately did not lead to vivianite formation, the proposed mechanism identifies an early microaeration window that favours phosphorus removal, providing a basis for further optimization of microaeration strategies for phosphorus recovery from anaerobic sludges.

title: Coupling structural-mineralization processes in the Tudui gold deposit, Jiaodong Peninsula: Constraints from pyrite trace elements and EBSD analysis
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Junjie Xu, Huan Li, Mohamed Faisal, Bowen Zhu, Wenbo Sun
abstract: Despite decades of research on hydrothermal gold systems, the micro-scale processes that govern the transition from initial gold precipitation to economic concentrations remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to predict ore formation. In the world-class Jiaodong gold province, the Tudui deposit provides an excellent case for investigating these processes using integrated microanalytical methods. In this contribution, we present the first integrated LA-ICP-MS trace element and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) microstructural analyses of pyrites from leptynites and diorite porphyry dikes in the study area to constrain the occurrence and enrichment mechanisms of gold. The pyrite Au-As relationship indicates that, in addition to previously identified visible gold, gold also occurs as invisible lattice-bound gold within pyrite. Trace element signatures suggest that the Tudui deposit is a hydrothermal gold system formed under epithermal, low-to-moderate temperature conditions, and Co/Ni ratios (0-81.1 ppm) together with Co/Sb-Se/Sb systematics are consistent with a mantle-derived fluid contribution. Discrimination diagrams based on Au-As/Sb and Se/Ge-Co/Ni demonstrate that gold precipitation was controlled by multiple coupled processes, including fluid-rock reaction, fluid boiling, and meteoric water mixing, which collectively destabilized Au(HS)2 - complexes and triggered gold deposition. EBSD results show that Tudui pyrites primarily experienced brittle deformation with subordinate plastic deformation, creating extensive microstructures and crystal defects that acted as favorable sites for gold deposition. These microstructures also established preferential pathways for trace element diffusion, enabling Au and other elements to migrate and precipitate along microfractures driven by chemical gradients between pyrite cores and rims. Overall, the Tudui deposit represents a structurally controlled, coupled metallogenic system. This study establishes an integrated macro-micro-scale model for mineralization in Jiaodong-type deposits and provides a theoretical basis for regional gold exploration in the Jiaodong Peninsula.

title: Photo-stimulated reductive dissolved Fe 2+ from epitaxial twinned goethite accelerated by fulvic acid: Insight from the band structure and photochemical activity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Shanshan Yang, Fei Liu, Xiao Ge, Hongrui Ding, Anhuai Lu
abstract: The photo-stimulated reductive dissolution of semiconducting iron (hydro)oxides plays a vital role in iron (bio)geochemistry processes. Epitaxial twinned goethite (Goe-Hem), a typical goethite twin composed of a hematite center with acicular goethite outgrowths, is widely distributed in natural environment. Nevertheless, studies exploring the photochemical activity of Goe-Hem remain limited. In this study, photo-stimulated reductive dissolution process of Goe-Hem were investigated in depth. Physicochemical characterization revealed that Goe-Hem consists of twinned goethite crystals with a hematite core, containing 73% goethite and 27% hematite. In the presence of fulvic acid, the concentration of photo-stimulated reductively dissolved Fe2+ (aq) from Goe-Hem was higher than that from goethite. Consequently, Goe-Hem exhibited superior photo-stimulated reductive ability than goethite. This enhanced activity was ascribed to the stronger visible light absorption, narrower band gap energy and more negative conduction band energy of Goe-Hem relative to goethite. The photo-stimulated reductively dissolved Fe2+ (aq) from Goe-Hem play a vital role in iron cycling and biological iron acquisition in nature.

title: Human activities as primary drivers of marine and inland groundwater salinization in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Christian Narvaez-Montoya, Saugata Datta, Jürgen Mahlknecht, Miguel Rangel-Medina
abstract: Groundwater salinization is a major threat to coastal aquifers worldwide, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions subjected to intensive groundwater use. Understanding the behavior of individual coastal aquifer systems is therefore essential to support effective groundwater management. This study evaluates the spatiotemporal salinization patterns of the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system, located at the coastal margin of the Sonoran Desert, using 357 groundwater samples collected in 2009 and 2016, primarily from the most productive and shallow hydrogeological unit. Multivariate and hydrogeochemical analyses suggest that seawater intrusion is the dominant driver of total dissolved solids and chloride enrichment, strongly linked to long-term overexploitation. Inland, heterogeneous nitrate and sulfate distributions suggest the influence of anthropogenic inputs, including urban wastewater infiltration and irrigation return flow. Temporal comparisons indicate a decrease in nitrate concentrations, likely reflecting improved wastewater treatment, alongside a significant increase in sulfate, which may be associated with enhanced water-rock interaction processes previously linked to irrigation practices. 15% of samples exceed drinking water guideline limits, and 47% exhibit poor irrigation water quality, highlighting potential risks for human consumption, soil salinization, and agricultural productivity. This study provides one of the most comprehensive recent assessments of salinization processes in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system and emphasizes the need to reduce groundwater abstraction and strengthen wastewater and irrigation management to prevent further degradation of the aquifer. Because the interpretations are based on major ions and previous studies, future investigations incorporating more sensitive tracers are needed to better constrain the mechanisms responsible for groundwater salinization.

title: Geochemical fractionation, mineralogical insights and environmental risk of toxic elements in mining-impacted soils of Zamfara State, Nigeria
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Jajati Mandal, Waheed Ariyo Bakare, Effiom Oku, Barnabas Iliya Musa, Abhishek Sharma, A.S.M. Fazle Bari, Michael D. Wood, Simon M. Hutchinson, Debapriya Mondal, Mohammad Mahmudur Rahman
abstract: This study examined the concentrations, geochemical partitioning, mineralogical controls, and probable mobility of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in mining impacted surface soils from Anka, Zamfara State, Nigeria. Soil samples (n = 50) were analyzed for physicochemical properties, total elemental burdens, and sequential extraction fractions. The soils ranged from sandy loam to clay loam and showed moderately acidic to near-neutral pH, elevated organic carbon, and high cation exchange capacity, reflecting substantial capacity for metal retention. Total elemental concentrations revealed lead (Pb) in the highest amount (1240.23 ± 92.94 mg kg−1), compared to arsenic (As), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), barium (Ba), and iron (Fe). Correlation studies indicated strong associations between Ba-Fe and Mn-Pb, suggesting shared mineralogical or oxide-based controls on distribution. Sequential extraction revealed marked differences in elemental mobility. Lead was primarily bound to reducible Fe-Mn oxides (∼83%), with only ∼13% in the extractable fraction. Arsenic was dominated by residual and oxidizable pools (>90%), indicating minimal mobility. However, Ba and Fe remained primarily in residual and reducible forms. In contrast, Zn was highly labile, with nearly 90% occurring in the extractable fraction displaying mixed extractable and reducible associations and reflecting its redox sensitivity. Mineralogical analyses confirmed quartz-dominant soils containing illite, muscovite, albite, galena, and Pb-As jarosite, with SEM-EDS further verifying PbS (galena), supporting the limited bioavailability of Pb in oxic conditions. Risk Assessment Code (RAC) values placed As in low-risk and Fe in the no-risk category, Ba in medium to high risk, Mn in high risk and Pb in medium risk, and Zn in very high risk (∼90%). Overall ecological risk ranking followed the order Zn > Mn > Ba > Pb > As > Fe. These findings highlight that while total Pb remains elevated, its mobility is restricted by mineralogical sinks, whereas Zn, despite low concentrations, exhibits high mobility and environmental responsiveness. These contrasting behaviours emphasize the need to interpret total elemental concentrations alongside geochemical fractionation when assessing contamination risk in mining-impacted landscapes.

title: Stable isotope fingerprints of Ni-Cu-PGE sulfide remobilization in Mesoarchean ultramafic-mafic rocks
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Shounak Dutta, Sisir K. Mondal
abstract: The origin of enigmatic Archean breccia-hosted Ni-Cu-PGE deposits is often debated because primary orthomagmatic and secondary hydrothermal mineralization can be difficult to distinguish. In this study, we investigate the Mesoarchean Nuasahi Ultramafic-Mafic Complex (India) using integrated petrology, mineral chemistry, and S-O-H isotope geochemistry to resolve the history of metal mobilization in its breccia zone. Our results data reveal a multi-stage mineralization process. An initial magmatic stage involved the interaction of a fluid-rich gabbroic melt with ultramafic-chromitite clasts, which induced sulfide liquid immiscibility and formed a high-temperature (∼950 °C) pyrrhotite–pentlandite–chalcopyrite assemblage with a mantle-like sulfur isotope composition (δ34S ∼ 0‰). The primary assemblage was later overprinted by hydrothermal alteration, characterised by the replacement of chromite by ferrianchromite and the growth of secondary pyrite-chalcopyrite at a lower temperature. Secondary chalcopyrite is selectively enriched in 34S (δ34S ∼ 1‰) relative to the primary pyrrhotite, producing pronounced isotopic disequilibrium. Oxygen and hydrogen isotopes in coexisting chlorite (δ18O ∼2.4‰; δD ∼ −28‰) indicate that the altering fluid resembled heated Archean seawater. We propose that the infiltration of this seawater remobilized primary sulfides, concentrating mobile chalcophile elements such as Pd. At the same time, the overall mantle-like sulfur signature was retained due to the low sulfate content of the Archean oceans. Selective sulfur-isotope disequilibrium in sulfide pairs thus provides a robust tracer of cryptic seawater-driven hydrothermal remobilization in ancient ultramafic-hosted ore systems.

title: Mineralogical and geochemical controls on Co-V-Pt-Ni enrichment in manganese mineralization: evidence from the Dilli deposit, Eastern Türkiye
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Mehmet Ali Gücer, Okay Çimen, Alican Aktağ, Serdar Keskin
abstract: The growing demand for critical minerals driven by the global energy transition and advanced technologies highlights the importance of unconventional metal reservoirs. This study investigates the Ni-, Co-, V-, and Pt-enriched Dilli manganese deposit (Kemaliye-Erzincan, Eastern Türkiye) to constrain the mineralogical, geochemical, and genetic controls on critical metal enrichment in Mn oxide mineralization. An integrated approach combining field observations, petrography, X-ray diffraction (XRD), whole-rock geochemistry, mineral chemistry, and stable C-O isotope analysis was applied to better understand the potential origin of critical mineral enrichments. The mineralization is dominated by Mn4+-bearing oxides, principally pyrolusite and hollandite, accompanied by minor rhodochrosite. High MnO (39-64 wt%) and very low Al2O3 and Fe2O3 contents indicate chemical precipitation with negligible detrital input. Discrimination diagrams and trace-element systematics consistently support a structurally controlled hydrothermal origin. Chondrite-normalized REE patterns display low total REE and very low Nd contents comparable to typical hydrothermal deposits, whereas neutral to slightly positive Ce anomalies and non-chondritic Y/Ho ratios suggest limited oxidative interaction with surface-derived fluids rather than primary marine hydrogenetic growth. Stable C–O isotope compositions of co-genetic calcite are inconsistent with a purely marine depositional environment and indicate precipitation from low-to moderate-temperature hydrothermal fluids. Mineral chemistry reveals strong phase-specific partitioning: hollandite preferentially incorporates V and Ba, whereas pyrolusite is enriched in Ni. Cobalt occurs in both phases, whereas Pt may also be present in both Mn oxide phases, suggesting that trace-element distribution is influenced by both crystallochemical and physicochemical controls. The enrichment of Ni, Co, and Pt is most plausibly linked to hydrothermal fluid circulation through ultramafic units, which likely acted as the primary metal source prior to precipitation. The Dilli deposit thus represents a structurally controlled hydrothermal Mn system enriched in critical metals, emphasizing the exploration relevance of Mn oxide mineral chemistry in identifying alternative sources of critical metals in Türkiye.

title: Relative kinetics of precipitation of barium chromate and barite in groundwater
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Abhas Singh, Mainak Bhattacharya, Ashwini Kumar Mohapatra
abstract: Water-soluble and carcinogenic hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] poses serious health risks due to its potential migration in aquifers and interaction with naturally present barium [Ba] to form sparingly soluble colloidal barium chromate [BaCrO4(s)]. However, Ba may also react with other solutes predominantly present in many groundwaters like dissolved sulfate [SO4], causing precipitation of barite [BaSO4(s)]. The eventual fate of Cr(VI) in such groundwaters may be governed by the relative rates of formation of these two solids, which are currently not known. In this contribution, simultaneous formation of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) in groundwater matrix and their relative kinetics were investigated through continuous flow stirred tank reactor experiments. Chromium-free Ba-spiked SO4-containing groundwater was introduced into the reactor, preloaded with Ba-free Cr(VI)-spiked SO4-containing groundwater, at a flow rate of 0.2 mL min−1. Aqueous samples were collected with time and analyzed for Cr(VI), SO4, Ba, and pH till steady-state was attained. Geochemical analysis of solute data and characterization of the precipitated solids confirmed rapid formation of a solid solution of ∼86 mol% BaCrO4(s) and ∼14 mol% BaSO4(s). Solution saturation indices with respect to BaCrO4(s) gradually decreased over time, but persistent supersaturation with BaSO4(s) suggested conditions favorable for formation of BaSO4(s). Time-dependent Cr(VI), SO4, and Ba concentrations were modelled with process-based mass balance equations. Optimized surface area normalized precipitation rate constants of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) were obtained as 6.3-8.6 × 10−8 mol m−2 s−1 and 1.3 × 10−8 mol m−2 s−1, respectively, indicating that BaCrO4(s) precipitates approximately five times faster than BaSO4(s). Determination of these constants would help in accurate prediction of Cr(VI) transport in contaminated aquifers rich in Ba and possibly similar co-solutes.

title: XAS evidence for Sb(V)-ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-magnetite during anoxic incubation of stormwater road basin sediments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Areej Adra, Maëva Philippe, Pierre Le Pape, Georges Ona-Nguema, Gautier Landrot, Ludovic Delbes, Elora Bourbon, Katell Quénéa, Sophie Ayrault
abstract: Antimony (Sb) presents versatile chemical forms in urban (sub)surface environments, the identity of which being driven by local redox conditions. Due to its use as additive in products for its flame-retardant properties, urban environments such as the Parisian area (Paris, France) are particularly subjected to Sb contamination. This is particularly observed in stormwater basin sediments, collecting Sb from runoff on road surfaces. Here, we used these sediments as a reactive ecosystem for aging Sb-bearing ferrihydrite, standing as a classical Sb carrier phase of surface environments and as possible input phase to the basins. Batch experiments were performed by mixing stormwater pond sediments plus Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite (Fh-Sb(V)) and were aged up to 210 days under a water column in oxic or anoxic conditions. For each series, an individual batch sample was sampled at 1, 7, 28 and 210 days of aging. Liquid samples were analyzed by ICP-MS, while Fe and Sb speciation were studied by X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES/EXAFS) to study Sb release to surface waters and the temporal evolution of Sb speciation. Whatever the experimental conditions, Sb release into solution remains below one percent of the initial stock introduced in the sediment, decorrelated of Fe(II) release and organic matter consumption during reduction processes. Under anoxic conditions, XANES data at the Fe K-edge show the transformation of ferrihydrite into magnetite. From EXAFS analysis at the Sb K-edge, we unambiguously identify a novel reaction route, Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-bearing magnetite, likely resulting from anoxic aging in a biotic medium. In the oxic experiment, diffusion of air through the initially anoxic water column resulted in the late oxidation of the newly Sb(III)-magnetite formed into Sb(V)-bearing phases. This study shows the strong geochemical reactivity of Sb when submitted to redox fluctuations and that iron-reducing activity likely drives Sb speciation in the presence of available Fe from poorly-crystalline ferrihydrite (Fh). Thus, the fundamental knowledge we bring here could help to define conditions propitious to limiting soluble Sb release from the solid phase in contaminated sediments submitted to redox fluctuations.

title: Uranium remobilization from a riparian wetland: Implications on long-term stewardship and extreme rain events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Daniel I. Kaplan, Karah M. Greene, Wei Xing, Arelis M. Rivera-Giboyeaux, Kenneth M. Kemner, Peng Lin
abstract: Natural attenuation of contaminants by wetlands can cause them to become secondary sources of contamination. The objectives of this field study were to: 1) measure the remobilization of uranium (U) in a stream flowing through a contaminated wetland in South Carolina, USA, and 2) develop empirical relationships between rainfall and U remobilization. Stream water was sampled hourly during six storm events ranging from 0.69 to 9.87 cm of rainfall, which caused flow to increase by as much as 1100% with respect to base flow. Uranium concentrations in all filtered samples, U < 0.45μm, were below the Maximum Contaminant Limit of 30 μg/L U. Conversely, as much as 94 vol% of the U in stream samples (g U/L streamwater) was associated with suspended solids, U ≥ 0.45μm. Consequently, significant correlations (p < 0.01) existed between stream water total U and suspended solids concentrations (or turbidity). Using a linear relationship (p < 0.01) between rainfall and remobilized U (g-U/sampling-event), it was estimated that 29% of the remobilized U in the year 2024 occurred during the three days of greatest rainfall. Similarly, using historical rainfall data, it was estimated that 864 kg-U, or 2.2% of the original 43,500 kg-U released into the wetland 55 years ago had been remobilized. This value of remobilized U is consistent with U-mass balance at the study site. Predictions of increased regional total rainfall and the number of extreme rainfall events may increase the rate of contaminant dispersion from riparian systems.

title: Harmful gas generation potential and disaster mechanisms in coastal sediments of Shenzhen Bay, China: Insights from geochemical characteristics and depositional environment
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Yuxuan Liu, Peidong Su, Peng Qiu, Yougui Li, Jun Sasaki
abstract: The flammability and toxicity of harmful gases pose significant safety risks during underground engineering construction. However, theoretical frameworks for the early-stage investigation of the generation potential and hazard mechanisms of shallow biogenic gases in coastal zones remain insufficient. In this study, three underground construction areas in the coastal zone of Shenzhen Bay, China, were selected as the research sites. Integrated organic and inorganic geochemical analyses were applied to systematically reconstruct the depositional environmental characteristics of the tunnel construction areas, evaluate potential for biogenic harmful gas generation, and explore their potential disaster mechanisms. The results indicate that the sediments in the study area contain relatively high organic matter with mixed terrestrial and marine sources and remain at a low maturity stage, providing favorable conditions for biogenic gas generation. In the Pearl River Estuary-Qianhai Bay tunnel construction site, the positive relationship between (Mo/U)EF and total sulfur (TS) suggests weak but episodic sulfidic conditions at the construction depth, likely associated with stronger hydrodynamic activity and lower sedimentation rates that facilitate sulfate penetration, indicating a higher potential for combined CH4-H2S hazards. In contrast, the Deep Bay tunnel site is characterized by weak hydrodynamics, high sedimentation rates, and strongly reducing conditions. The weakly correlated relationship between (Mo/U)EF and TS indicates dominance of methanogenesis, suggesting a methane-dominated hazard potential. Finally, a conceptual investigation framework for biogenic harmful gases in coastal underground engineering is proposed to support early risk identification and prevention.

title: Differential responses of vanadate reduction to soil aggregate types
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Zhenhan Li, Song Wang, Fengyuan Zhuang, Qinghao Zhang, Baogang Zhang
abstract: Different soil aggregate fractions create distinct biogeochemical microhabitats, driving divergent ecological adaptations and functional traits. In this study, different aggregate fractions from a vanadium-contaminated soil were inoculated into the reactors to evaluate their differences in pentavalent vanadium [V(V)] reduction capacity. Micro-aggregates (MiA) achieved the highest V(V) removal efficiency of 96.2 ± 0.12% and the fastest first-order removal kinetics (rate constant 0.06 h−1), followed by medium aggregates, small aggregates, and large aggregates. The microbial consortia from aggregate could transform toxic soluble V(V) into less mobile tetravalent vanadium [V(IV)] precipitates, thereby contributing to the remediation of vanadium-contaminated soil. During the V(V) reduction process, microbial communities underwent significant changes, exhibiting lower richness and diversity and forming a distinct cluster compared to the initial samples. Meanwhile, the relative abundance of metal-reducing genera increased from 5.29 ± 0.79% to 39.2 ± 12.3%. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed tight microbial collaboration, whereas larger aggregate fractions were associated with lower V(V) removal efficiency. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that V(V) reduction genes were potentially associated with reductive metabolism and electron transfer genes. The microbiome in MiA exhibited the highest cytochrome c levels and the strongest expression of potential V(V) reduction genes of omcB and narG, highlighting microorganisms derived from MiA-aggregates as primary drivers of vanadium detoxification in contaminated soils.

title: Phase-specific particle size distributions in Hanford tank waste measured by automated SEM–EDS: A statistical comparison across a waste column
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 209 Author(s): Edgar C. Buck, Austin A. Bachman, Jarrod R. Allred, Carolyn A.M. Burns, Amy M. Westesen, Reid A. Peterson
abstract: This study supports in-tank sludge washing and delivery of initial feed to the Hanford High-Level Waste vitrification facility by characterizing particle populations in 241-AN-106 wastes from the southeast quadrant of the Hanford Site. We developed computational tools to determine particle size distributions for specific mineralogical phases within these heterogeneous sludges. Automated Particle Analysis (APA), combining scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), was used to quantify particle morphology and composition for tens of thousands of individual particles, providing phase-resolved particle size distributions that are more representative than manual measurements. Phase-specific size distributions were compared among positions within a series of 241-AN-106 core-samples, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic was applied to test for statistically significant differences. Results demonstrate measurable size separation of gibbsite particle populations with position within the sludge layers, where larger gibbsite particles partitioned to the lower segments. This study illustrates how high-throughput, phase-resolved particle sizing can improve understanding of waste heterogeneity relevant to washing and feed delivery.

title: Analyzing phosphorus flow in crop production via interpretable machine learning: Insights from a typical agricultural region of Jiangxi Province, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yuejin Chen, Wending Huang, Lele Ru, Shuhui Peng, Wuhu Guo, Evgeny Abakumov, Ekaterina Chebykina, Yalan Zhang, Zanxu Chen, Dan Wang, Shijie Dai, Yanqi Liu, Huoqing Xiao, Monan Shao, Wei Liu, Zugen Liu, Xianchuan Xie
abstract: Understanding historical phosphorus (P) cycling in crop production is essential for sustainable P management and water quality protection. This study adopts a comprehensive perspective of the crop production process, focusing on Jiangxi Province, an intensively farmed region in China. A bottom-up, multi-year dynamic phosphorus substance flow analysis (P-SFA) model was developed considering regional social diversity and P flow complexity. The P cycle in Jiangxi shifted from a natural-dominated steady state to a human-driven unidirectional system, with major changes occurring between 1978 and 2015. Agricultural intensification and livestock expansion have continuously increased P flows in the region. Total P input rose from 5.84 × 104 t in 1950 to 2.13 × 105 t in 2020, representing an almost fourfold increase. Since 1950, chemical fertilizers became the largest P source, reaching 1.25 × 105 t (58.86% of total) in 2020. Interpretability-based machine learning (ML) model quantified the influence of P flow drivers. SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis confirmed that agriculture accounts for over 75% of P flow intensity, highlighting key socio-economic factors. This nonlinear identification method offers a new perspective for SFA. The SFA–ML model improves understanding of P flows and their role in watershed P cycling.

title: Speciation transformation and (im)mobilization of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenic in river sediment environments: impact of leaf litter
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Li Zhang, Bolin Li, Hulong Yi, Qianhua Chen, Tianci Liu, Jianqiao Wang, Enzong Xiao, Yi Wang, Jinli Cui
abstract: Plant leaf litter substantially increases the content and diversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in river sediment environments and may influence the mobility and transformation of arsenic (As), but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, microcosm incubations of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate in simulated river sediment environments, supplemented with tree leaf litter, were employed. During the incubations, the amount of arsenic initially released from the spent ferrihydrite materials into solution continuously decreased. Speciation analysis revealed the dominance of arsenate (98.5–100%) and lesser amounts of arsenite (0.9–1.5%) in the solution of all incubations. In the sequential extraction of solid fractions, water-extractable fraction contributed <1.0% and arsenite reached 39.4–100% in the presence of sediment and 86.8-100% in the presence of leaves or coexisting leaves and sediment. Arsenic in the solid phase was predominantly associated with amorphous (24.2–45.1%) and crystalline iron (oxyhydr)oxide fractions (54.1–75.7%). The iron (oxyhydr)oxide-associated arsenic was dominated by arsenate (92.2–100%), whereas arsenite was observed only in the presence of coexisting leaves and sediment at the end of incubation, reaching 3.6–7.8%. Coupled with the observation of ferrous iron in the amorphous and crystalline iron fractions, these findings confirm the reduction of iron and arsenic in the ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate material in sediment environments following leaf litter deposition. Fluorescence analysis confirmed that leaf-derived DOM contained terrestrial humic-like components, microbial humic-like components, and protein-like components, which strongly controlled As sorption behavior, likely via competitive interactions and DOM-mediated reactions, including the adsorption properties and reductive transformation of iron (oxyhydr)oxides. Compared with the control, leaf-derived DOM facilitated arsenate reduction largely via microbial processes (99.9%) mediated by sedimentary microbes. Metagenomic analysis further supported that iron/arsenate reduction was potentially driven by specific dissimilatory respiration genes for Fe (e.g., pilA) and As (e.g., arrAB) and the detoxifying arsenate reductase gene (arsC) identified in Geobacter and Pseudomonas. This study demonstrated that reactive leaf-derived DOM can be substantially involved in the microbial redox transformation of arsenic and iron in riverine sediment scenarios.

title: Mineralogy and geochemistry of beach sediments in the Gulf of Mexico and Mexican Pacific: Implication for provenance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Barbara Y. Pérez-Alvarado, John S. Armstrong-Altrin, Itzamna Z. Flores-Ocampo, Gloria D. Fernández-Guevara
abstract: This study assesses the geochemical characteristics and provenance of sediments from four beaches in the Gulf of Mexico (Barra Norte and Mocambo) and Mexican Pacific coast (Puerto Chiapas and Acapulco). Major, trace, and rare earth element (REE) concentrations with textural parameters were analysed to identify the sediment provenance and its associated geodynamic processes. Grain-size analysis revealed marked textural differences, with the domination of coarse-grained sediments in Acapulco, medium-grained sediments in Puerto Chiapas, and fine-grained sediments in Mocambo and Barra Norte beaches. Quartz dominates the mineral assemblages in all beaches, although Puerto Chiapas and Mocambo sediments contain higher proportions of mafic minerals, Acapulco and Barra Norte exhibit predominantly of felsic assemblages. Major-element geochemistry reveals strong compositional contrasts among three beaches. Puerto Chiapas sediments are enriched in Fe2O3, MgO, Cr, V, and Ni, indicating intermediate to mafic provenance, whereas Acapulco sediments exhibit high SiO2 contents (84.6-87.4 wt %), consistent with felsic and compositionally mature sedimentary sources. In contrast, Barra Norte and Mocambo sediments are characterized by elevated CaO contents associated with carbonate input, as well as felsic and intermediate source rocks. The chondrite-normalized REE patterns show LREE enrichment in all samples. CIA and PIA values indicate overall low chemical weathering in the three beaches, with slightly higher alteration in Puerto Chiapas (CIA and PIA ≈ 57) compared to Acapulco, Mocambo, and Barra Norte beaches (CIA and PIA ≈ 41-49), reflecting the preservation of relatively unaltered feldspars. Elemental ratios like Al2O3/TiO2, Cr and Ni contents, and the size of the Eu anomaly suggest a felsic source for the Acapulco, and Barra Norte sediments, whereas Mocambo and Puerto Chiapas sediments reflect intermediate provenance with minor mafic contributions. The geoaccumulation index (Igeo) and enrichment factor (EF) indicate that the beach sediments are practically uncontaminated (Igeo < 0; EF < 2), except a moderate enrichment is observed for Co, Zn, and V in some Puerto Chiapas samples, collected near to the seaport. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) results indicate that major and trace elements variability is partly controlled by grain-size and heavy-minerals, while REE distributions are independent of grain size. The results of this study further indicate a diverse provenance, with contributions from mafic to intermediate source rocks for the Puerto Chiapas and Mocambo, and predominantly felsic source rocks for the Acapulco and Barra Norte beaches. These findings demonstrate that sediment geochemistry along the Mexican coastal areas is primarily controlled by source-rock lithology, regional tectonic setting, and hydrodynamic sorting.

title: Element-selective colloid-facilitated transport of radionuclides by C–S–H nanoparticles in porous concrete columns
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Hyeonjin Eun, Seungmo Yeon, Jisoo Jung, Hyeongjin Kim, Hee-Kyung Kim, Jong-Il Yun
abstract: Colloid-facilitated transport has been recognized as an important factor influencing radionuclide transport, but studies in cementitious systems remain limited. Batch sorption and column transport experiments were conducted using Cs(I), Se(IV), Mo(VI), and U(VI) to investigate radionuclide transport facilitated by C–S–H colloids in porous concrete columns. C–S–H colloids were synthesized using a double precipitation method in the presence of polycarboxylate ether (PCE).
