The results showed spatiotemporal variations with upstream sites decreasing from 82,222 ± 28,958 MPs/m3 in summer 2023 to 63,444 ± 19,777 MPs/m3 in winter 2024, while as downstream sites increased from 21000 ± 11737 MPs/m3 in winter 2023 to 44,333 ± 10,456 MPs/m3 in summer 2024. Fibers were the most dominant morphology (94.93 %), with size distribution mainly in the range of (<75 µm–4 µm) at 36 %. Estimated daily releases of microplastics from untreated MSW landfill leachate was recorded with 2.24 × 10 6 M P s d a y - 1 (MPD) in 2023 and 6.30 × 10 6 M P s d a y - 1 (MPD) in 2024. Uncommon polymers such as PTFE and CR were detected in downstream region, confirming landfill origin contamination. Risk assessment indicated an overall Pollution Load Index (PLI) of 3.2 (hazard category I, low risk), Polymer Hazard Index (PHI) of 21.34 (hazard category II, medium risk) and Potential Ecological Risk Index (PERI) values between 4185 ± 6724 and 8796 ± 13,952 (extreme danger risk category). Chronic Daily Intake (CDI) and Incremental Lifetime Cancer Risk (ILCR) exposure assessments show higher exposure and cancer risk for children than adults. Our study provides evidence that untreated landfill leachate and laundry effluents intensify microplastic pollution and ecological risks in the interconnected freshwater systems.

title: Optimising river sampling and load calculation methods for total phosphorus: influence of catchment size and population
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Maëlle Fresne, Phil Jordan, Raymond Wilson, Rachel Cassidy
abstract: Reliable estimates of river nutrient load are critical benchmarks for catchment and receiving waterbody management. Low-frequency monitoring is known to underestimate phosphorus (P) loads in small catchments, yet performance in large catchments, sometimes including large urban areas, remains poorly evaluated. This study used synchronous sub-daily river discharge and concentration datasets from three catchments of contrasting size and population to evaluate how these characteristics influence the performance of sampling and load calculation methods for total P load estimation. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to assess the impact of catchment size and population on load estimate accuracy, with bias and precision derived from accuracy distributions. Sampling method performance was strongly dependent on catchment size and, less consistently, population. The smaller, flashier, and lower-population catchments required higher-frequency sampling to better capture short-duration runoff events and temporally variable diffuse inputs, which likely contributed to a greater proportion of total loads. The larger, higher-population catchment produced better load estimates under lower-frequency sampling, likely due to steadier point source contributions. While load calculation method performance varied with catchment population, flow-weighting was the most robust approach. However, even when combined with this approach, low-frequency sampling in the large catchments resulted in biased or imprecise load estimates: for example, a standard weekly sampling produced minimal bias (-7.0%–+2.1%) but poor precision (20.3%–72.8%). The findings reveal the need to adapt monitoring protocols to catchment characteristics and to increase monitoring frequency in large rivers to at least daily (ideally 7-hourly) to better support effective catchment and waterbody management.

title: Domain-knowledge-guided deep learning for probabilistic precipitation downscaling over southeastern Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Dayang Li, Baoxiang Pan, Yuan Liu, Ashish Sharma, Yan Zhou, Yi Yao, Jun Yin, Long Yang
abstract: Precipitation downscaling, particularly at convection-permitting scales, is highly uncertain. This is especially pronounced in mountainous regions, such as the Tibetan Plateau (TP), due to the complex topography and atmospheric dynamics, hindering reliable estimation of variability and risk in extreme localized rainstorms. Deep learning-based downscaling methods have gained increasing attention but have primarily focused on deterministic results, which fail to capture uncertainty. Here we proposed a Probabilistic High-resolution Precipitation Downscaling Network (P-HPDNet) by incorporating domain knowledge of key precipitation characteristics to guide its loss function and model architecture. The negative log-likelihood loss function was derived to address zero-inflation, high skewness, and heteroscedasticity in the precipitation distribution. The model architecture incorporates convolutional layers, long short-term memory network layers, and spatial attention mechanisms to capture spatial and temporal precipitation dependencies. P-HPDNet was tested over southeastern TP, a mountainous region lacking high-resolution precipitation data. A ten-year dataset of daily precipitation data at 9-km and 1-km resolutions was derived from Weather Research and Forecasting model simulations to train P-HPDNet. Compared with a baseline model that lacks domain knowledge guidance, P-HPDNet reduces the continuous ranked probability score by 28% for all precipitation values, with an even larger reduction of 55% for extreme precipitation. Furthermore, P-HPDNet was applied to downscale a satellite-based precipitation product without retraining, demonstrating significant improvements in capturing both temporal and spatial dependencies of precipitation. Our study highlights the importance of incorporating domain knowledge of precipitation characteristics into deep learning models, offering an efficient downscaling approach for regions with complex terrains.

title: SURGIN : SUR rogate-guided G enerative IN version for subsurface multiphase flow with quantified uncertainty
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Zhao Feng, Bicheng Yan, Luanxiao Zhao, Xianda Shen, Renyu Zhao, Wenhao Wang, Fengshou Zhang
abstract: We present a direct inverse modeling method named SURGIN, a SURrogate-guided Generative INversion framework tailored for subsurface multiphase flow data assimilation. Unlike existing inversion methods that require adaptation for each new observational configuration, SURGIN features a zero-shot conditional generation capability, enabling real-time assimilation of unseen monitoring data without task-specific retraining. Specifically, SURGIN synergistically integrates a U-Net enhanced Fourier Neural Operator (U-FNO) surrogate with a score-based generative model (SGM), framing the conditional generation as a surrogate prediction-guidance process in a Bayesian perspective. Instead of directly learning the conditional generation of geological parameters, an unconditional SGM is first pretrained in a self-supervised manner to capture the geological prior, after which posterior sampling is performed by leveraging a differentiable U-FNO surrogate to enable efficient forward evaluations conditioned on unseen observations. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate SURGIN’s capability to effectively infer heterogeneous geological fields and predict spatiotemporal flow dynamics with quantified uncertainty across diverse measurement settings. Benchmark comparisons with classic Bayesian inversion baselines further demonstrate improved posterior reconstruction and uncertainty characterization. By unifying generative learning with surrogate-guided Bayesian inference, SURGIN establishes a new paradigm for inverse modeling and uncertainty quantification in parametric function spaces.

title: Integrating scale-matched spatial scales into water scarcity risk screening in China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Jiayu Zhang, Dedi Liu, Jiabo Yin, Feng Yue, Jiaoyang Wang, Zhenyu Mu, Hanxu Liang, Zhilin Niu, Zhengbo Peng
abstract: Effective water scarcity assessment is frequently challenged by spatial mismatches between fine-resolution hydrologic water supply and administratively aggregated water-use statistics, which can obscure spatial heterogeneity and reduce the interpretability of results for planning. To address this spatial mismatch, a scale-matched framework is proposed for water scarcity risk screening by coupling multi-scale water demand simulation with runoff-derived renewable potential supply. Water demand is simulated by spatially explicit variables via a cellular automata (CA) model to produce gridded water demand at three scales: 1 km × 1 km scale, the appropriate spatial scale, and prefecture scale. Runoff-derived renewable potential supply is derived as runoff depth multiplied by a regionally specified water resources exploitation ratio, and this potential is also expressed as gridded fields at the three scales. Water scarcity risk screening indicators are then computed on these scale-matched grids and subsequently aggregated into basin and administrative units. The resulting scale-matched water scarcity risk signals are quantified by three complementary indicators—deficit ratio, temporal reliability, and non-deficit fraction, which characterize the mismatch magnitude, the long-horizon stability, and the spatial prevalence of non-water scarcity conditions, respectively. Results indicate that screening signals are systematically altered across the three different scales: the 1 km × 1 km scale reveals fragmented high-pressure clusters, the appropriate spatial scale retains coherent regional patterns while preserving meaningful sub-unit contrasts, and prefecture-scale aggregation yields smoother signals but can mask localized risk pockets. Persistently screened hotspots are concentrated in demand-intensive corridors such as the North China Plain and in arid inland systems in the Northwest, with strengthened screening signals toward end-century conditions in parts of the Northwest and the Southwest. Overall, a reproducible, scale-consistent screening tool designed to support spatial prioritization, basin–administrative coordination, and targeted planning diagnostics.

title: A hybrid decision-support framework for managing salt intrusion via controlled freshwater pulses in regulated estuaries
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Guillermo Martín-Llanes, Erwan Garel, Alejandro López-Ruiz
abstract: Managing salt intrusion in estuaries is critical given increasing freshwater scarcity and human-induced salinization. This study presents a transferable hybrid framework to support salt intrusion management in regulated estuaries, combining a three-dimensional Delft3D-Flow model with parameterized analytical equations for predicting salt intrusion under varying discharge. Model implementation is based on estuarine domains with idealized geometries, reducing human-resource demands while enhancing accessibility and reproducibility. The steady intrusion equation follows Hansen and Rattray (1966), whereas the unsteady intrusion equation follows Monismith (2017). The framework is demonstrated in the Guadiana Estuary and applied to: (1) identify the key variables controlling the salinity response to short-duration freshwater pulses, and (2) optimize freshwater-release strategies based on limited freshwater volumes. Results highlight the critical role of background flow over pulse configuration (i.e., peak discharge and duration) when pulse volume is constant: the period during which salt intrusion remains below x = 47 km varies from 29 to 55 days as background flow increases from 6 to 8 m3 s−1, while increasing peak discharge from 300 to 1800 m3 s−1 extends that period by one day. For a fixed freshwater volume of 45 hm3 and a background flow of 4 m3 s−1, optimized release strategies yield maximum control durations of 15–125 days for intrusion threshold values between 30 and 50 km, respectively. Overall, the framework offers a practical decision-support tool that enhances stakeholder engagement in water resource and salt intrusion management, particularly by enabling rapid optimization of freshwater-release strategies under limited freshwater availability and user-defined salinity thresholds.

title: Spatio-Temporal Evolution Analysis of Flood-Chain Disasters for Water Diversion Project Safety
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Lihu Wang, Xuemei Liu, Hairui Li, Xiaonan Chen, Libo Yang
abstract: Water diversion projects are highly coupled complex systems, and under the combined influence of extreme rainfall and complex operating conditions, flood disasters exhibit pronounced chain propagation effects, posing significant challenges to disaster prevention and control. This study integrates large models with knowledge graphs to analyze the spatio-temporal evolution patterns of flood-chain disasters. Based on multiscale decomposition and reconstruction, a representation-enhanced large model is developed to enhance the capability to analyze non-stationary data, enabling trend prediction and anomaly detection for rainfall and runoff. The coupling characteristics of different disaster events are quantified to construct a disaster knowledge graph that characterizes the chain propagation of extreme rainfall, abnormal runoff, and engineering accidents. Multi-chain coupled disaster reasoning techniques are studied to integrate features from different disaster chains, revealing the impact of flood-chain disasters on engineering safety during their spatio-temporal evolution. The proposed method was validated using 4,814,708 rainfall and runoff observations and 6853 inspection records. The results show that the proposed method outperforms in trend prediction and accident recognition, with mean MAE and F1 scores of 174.5 and 0.751, respectively. Flood disaster chains exhibit superimposition, diffusion, and asymmetry, with abnormal station levels and engineering accident levels showing temporal correlations and spatial clustering characteristics. This study accomplished the spatio-temporal analysis of flood-chain disasters, expanding the technical framework for disaster research in water diversion projects and providing support for safety early warning.

title: Elevation-dependent hydrological vulnerability of lakes and reservoirs to evaporation loss in the Yarlung Zangbo River Basin, Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Chengwei Wan, Chenghao Chen, Grzegorz Skrzypek, John J. Gibson, Xuegao Chen, Xiang Xu, Peng Yi, Kei Yoshimura, Hayoung Bong, Xicai Pan
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau’s Yarlung Zangbo River Basin is undergoing rapid hydroclimatic transitions compounded by extensive reservoir development. Accurately quantifying evaporative water losses and water balance and interpreting their associated isotopic signatures is critical for improving hydrological models and regional water security assessment. In this study, we tested the application of an isotope-based Bayesian framework for quantifying evaporation and water balance dynamics. Utilizing steady-state models for the long-term water balance of natural lakes and transient models for the short-term water balance of artificial reservoirs, this framework calculated a unified mass-balance metric, the evaporative loss index (E/(E+Q)), where E represents evaporative water loss and Q denotes water outflow. Results reveal that despite operating on different temporal scales, the inflow-dependent evaporative loss indices exhibit diametrically opposed altitudinal dependencies between lakes and reservoirs, which can substantially mask the natural riverine δ 18O altitude effect. Natural lakes, for which evaporative loss index is functionally equivalent to the evaporation-to-inflow ratio under steady-state conditions, are found to have average values of 0.27 ± 0.19 and show a strong positive correlation with elevation. In high-altitude basins (> 4500 m a.s.l.), limited natural inflows cause substantial proportional evaporative losses relative to the water balance (mean E/(E+Q) = 0.51), highlighting severe hydrological vulnerability to evaporative loss despite low absolute evaporation rates. This intense fractionation can substantially modify the pristine cryospheric baseflow, acting as a contributing mechanism to the reversal of the steep negative gradient in localized surface waters.. Conversely, artifically-constructed reservoirs exhibit a negative altitudinal evaporative gradient, with evaporation accounting for 0.47 ± 0.16 of total water losses in low-elevation shallow basins during the dry season. Rapid downstream transport of water from high-altitude reservoirs disrupts and homogenizes natural isotopic gradients in rivers. This systematic disruption of natural isotopic baselines by both climate-driven evaporation and human water retention explicitly warns against utilizing uncorrected surface water isotopes for hydrological tracing or paleoaltimetry reconstructions. These findings highlight extreme vulnerabilities in regional water security, demanding altitude-specific management adaptations.

title: A Bellman equation-based unified framework for evaluating and optimizing reservoir hedging rules: Incorporating inflow temporal dependence and non-stationary environments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Ximeng Xu, Chao Ma, Haixing Gou
abstract: Hedging rules (HRs) are widely used in reservoir operation due to their simplicity and strong theoretical basis. However, their practical application is constrained by restrictive assumptions, such as predetermined differentiable utility functions, temporally independent inflows, and stationary environments. This study addresses these limitations by formulating reservoir operation as a Markov decision process and developing a unified hedging framework based on the Bellman equation. First, the Bellman expectation equation is utilized to calculate value functions for given HRs, establishing a quantitative criterion for rule comparison. Second, the Bellman optimality equation is utilized to derive the optimal value functions and corresponding optimal HRs. Third, comprehensive theoretical analysis and numerical experiments are carried out for optimal value functions and optimal HRs. Both Markovian inflow cases and non-stationary environments are studied, yielding two-dimensional HRs and time-varying HRs, respectively. Key properties such as monotonicity, concavity, and convergence of the optimal value function are derived. A detailed parameter sensitivity analysis examines how optimal HRs respond to variations in reservoir storage capacity, discount factor, discharge utility function, inflow distribution characteristics, and temporal dependence. This unified framework supports both the evaluation and optimization of HRs, strengthening the theory of reservoir hedging.

title: A study on sediment forecasting using machine learning with structure-aware mechanisms
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yanmeng Zhang, Shengqi Jian, Faxian Liang, Huiliang Wang, Shentang Dou, Xin Yu
abstract: In recent years, machine learning has been widely applied in sediment forecasting; however, existing research has largely focused on the model algorithms themselves, with insufficient integration of the mechanistic characteristics of sediment transport processes (such as the response mechanism of sediment peaks and time-lag effects). This has resulted in limited forecasting capabilities for sudden sediment peaks in complex river basins. To address the challenge of highly abrupt and spatio-temporally variable sediment transport processes in the typical high-sediment- concentration basin of the middle Yellow River, this study proposes a machine learning model for sediment forecasting (ML-P-EF) incorporating a structural enhancement mechanism. Building upon LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), ANN (Artificial Neural Network) and Transformer models, systematically incorporates Sediment Process Vectorization (SPV), Dynamic Lag Encoding (DLE) and Event-Driven Features (EDF) to enhance the model’s ability to perceive and simulate sediment physical processes. Through validation in typical catchment areas of the Jing River and Beiluo River in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, taking Hongde Station as an example, for a 1-hour forecast horizon, the ANN-P-EF model achieved a Nash efficiency coefficient (NSE) of 0.97 and a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 52.31 kg∙m⁻3, and the peak sediment error was –3.81 %. Under a 6-hour forecast horizon, the NSE of the LSTM-P-EF model improved by more than 40 % compared to the LSTM-P and LSTM models, the RMSE decreased by over 50 %, and the peak error was reduced by 6 %–12 %. This study innovatively integrates the mechanisms of sediment transport processes with deep learning models, enhancing the model’s ability to capture the non-linear response of sediment peaks. It provides a new technical approach to accurate sediment forecasting in high-sediment river basins, with significant implications for regional water and sediment management as well as disaster prevention and mitigation.

title: Ecohydrological thresholds of alpine meadow slopes: Quantifying resilience limits under a warming-wetting climate
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Haitao Zhao, Zhihong Zhang, Yanchen Guo, Fuchu Dai
abstract: Alpine meadow vegetation (AMV) acts as a critical ecohydrological buffer in the cryosphere, playing a pivotal role in modulating active layer dynamics and mitigating shallow slope instability. However, the accelerating warming and wetting trend on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) is profoundly altering this hydro-thermal regime, yet the quantitative limits of such ecohydrological regulation remain unclear. This study investigates the complex feedback within the “climate-vegetation-soil” system by developing a process-based hydro-thermal coupled model that explicitly integrates root water uptake (RWU) and heat absorption functions. Unlike traditional approaches that simplify vegetation as mechanical reinforcement, our framework utilizes root biomass to characterize the vertical decay of root distribution, enabling precise simulation of soil moisture redistribution and phase change dynamics in frozen ground. Results demonstrate that alpine meadows exert a significant hydro-thermal buffering effect, reducing shallow soil temperatures by 0.13°C-0.42°C and peak volumetric water content (VWC) by 1.0%-2.6% through transpiration and shading. While this regulation enhances slope stability (safety factor increases by 3%-10%), we identified a critical hydrological tipping point. Under a coupled warming (+0.33°C) scenario, the critical rainfall intensity threshold for stability contracts from 5 mm/h to approximately 4 mm/h. Beyond this limit, excessive infiltration overwhelms the canopy’s bio-drainage capacity, rendering slope failure inevitable. These findings quantify the physical tipping points of ecohydrological regulation in the cryosphere, offering a critical scientific benchmark for optimizing Nature-based Solutions (NbS) against the non-linear risks of a warming-wetting climate.

title: Projected depletion of high mountain Asia glaciers by 2100: linking mass loss to asynchronous peak runoff
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Muhammad Mannan Afzal, Fuming Xie, Yu Zhu, Adeel Ahmad Nadeem, Fazli Hameed, Yi Luo, Tandong Yao, Fubao Sun, Xin Wang, Qiao Liu, Jyoti Karki, Jun Zhou, Shiyin Liu
abstract: Glacierized-catchment runoff (GR) across High Mountain Asia (HMA) is approaching peak water, but the timing is not uniform. Glacier size, elevation, and regional climate push that threshold to different points in time, with direct implications for downstream water security. We used OGGM v1.6.1, forced by bias-corrected GSWP3-W5E5 historical data and an ensemble of 13 CMIP6 GCMs under 4 SSP scenarios, to simulate glacier mass balance, dynamics, and glacierized-catchment runoff across 17 major HMA basins from 1940 to 2100. By 2100, HMA-wide glacier mass declines by 70.7 ± 9.6%, relative to 2000 levels, and total GR falls by 10 ± 6.5% between the early (2001–2020) and late (2081–2100) century periods. Small, low-elevation glaciers have already passed peak runoff in many basins, some before 2020, and are losing volume rapidly. Large, high-elevation glaciers continue buffering downstream flows well into the late 21st century, with basin-wide peaks as late as 2058 in Tarim and 2064 in the Amu Darya, and individual large high-elevation glacier classes peaking as late as 2083 in Tarim under high-emission scenarios. We identify three distinct peak-GR regimes: early, transitional, and delayed, driven by the size and elevation composition of glacier classes within each basin, rather than average glacier behavior. Basin-averaged projections may obscure important class-specific runoff transitions, underscoring the need for class-resolved, basin-specific water resource planning across HMA.

title: Flood-generating mechanism attribution across U.S. catchments: the role of soil-layer depth and framework sensitivity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Bin Zhang, Nergui Nanding, Huan Wu, Zhijun Huang, Yan Yan, Weitian Chen
abstract: Floods arise from diverse hydroclimatic drivers, yet flood-mechanism attribution often relies on a single diagnostic framework and simplified representations of catchment storage, leaving cross-framework consistency and the role of antecedent-storage representation poorly understood. Here, we compare three diagnostically distinct attribution frameworks, including circular statistics, rule-based classification, and interpretable machine learning, across 542 minimally regulated catchments in the conterminous United States using a consistent flood-event sampling strategy, hydrometeorological datasets, and a common set of mechanism categories. We further evaluate how soil-layer depth representation influences attribution of Soil-moisture Excess (SE) floods. Across all three frameworks, SE emerges as the dominant flood-generating mechanism, contributing 33–35% of total mechanism importance, and prevailing across much of the southeastern United States. Long-rainfall (LR) also contributes substantially, whereas Snowmelt (SM) and Rain-on-snow (RS) remain concentrated primarily in mountainous and high-latitude regions. Despite this broad consistency, substantial cross-framework divergence exists in inferred magnitudes of mechanism importance. Circular statistics produces highly concentrated “all-or-nothing” attributions, rule-based classification assigns comparatively stronger RS contributions, and machine learning identifies consistently larger Short-rainfall (SR) contributions through conditional predictive relationships. Attribution results also show strong sensitivity to soil-layer representation. Deepening the soil column reduces SE importance in rule-based process classification and machine learning frameworks, whereas circular statistics shows a non-monotonic response associated with seasonal timing alignment and attribution-solver sensitivity. These findings demonstrate that flood-mechanism attribution is inherently framework dependent and sensitive to antecedent-storage representation, with important implications for flood-frequency analysis, flood-risk assessment, and climate-change attribution of flood events.

title: Climate-informed streamflow forecasting based on a Bayesian autoregressive exogenous stochastic volatility model and its use for hydrological drought forecasting
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Pamela Sofia Fabian, Hemie Cho, Yoo-Geun Ham, Hyun-Han Kwon
abstract: In the context of South Korea’s recurring drought challenges, this study explores season-ahead predictability of hydrological drought, focusing on Bayesian autoregressive modeling incorporating stochastic volatility. To better understand uncertainty, our approach integrates Bayesian inference and stochastic volatility, with comparisons of conventional autoregressive (AR), autoregressive with exogenous variables (ARX), and autoregressive exogenous with stochastic volatility (ARXSV) models. Our study explores the integration of climate-based information with statistical modeling, presenting a comprehensive framework for water resource management. We aim to predict June–July–August (JJA) streamflow and to assess the influence of large-scale climate predictors, such as the sea surface temperature and sea level pressure associated with the North Atlantic Oscillation. The methodology encompasses exploratory data analyses, the use of hydrological drought indices, and considerations related to dam operation. The research provides tailored season-ahead streamflow forecasts specifically for the critical monsoon season JJA, where hydrometeorological variability is paramount. By incorporating climate information within a Bayesian inference framework and stochastic volatility, we show that the proposed approach outperforms conventional autoregressive models, providing decision-makers with an efficient tool to address climate risk and support dam operation planning, ultimately contributing to improved water-resources management.

title: Beyond proportional training set selection in data-driven models: A novel two side distributional decomposition method for urban flood prediction
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Songhua Huan
abstract: Data-driven models have emerged as promising solutions for urban flood prevention. However, the training set selection adopted in most model designs primarily relies on fixed proportion, bringing additional uncertainty for accuracy. In this study, a Two Side Distributional Decomposition (TSDD) is proposed for non-proportional training set selection in urban flood prediction. Experimental results based on urban drainage water level data show that: (1) TSDD achieves better performance across four models including tree-based (RF), recurrent-based (LSTM), convolution-based (CNN), and attention-based (Transformer) data-driven models when integrated with six decomposition methods (EMD, SEMD, VMD, SVMD, STL, SSTL) under diverse experimental settings. The average R2 across all urban drainage stations reaches 0.928. Specifically, the average R2 for lower, middle, and upper reaches are 0.969, 0.859, and 0.956, respectively. (2) TSDD exhibits good abilities in processing high-frequency flood data. Flood data sampled at 2-minutes frequency yields better accuracy in most stations with an average R2 of 0.933, compared to an average R2 of 0.929 for 10-minutes frequency. (3) TSDD enables higher accuracy with fewer data resources. It may deliver good performance using a smaller number of labeled training samples instead of traditional proportional selection like 80%. This study may enhance a multi-rules training set selection in urban flood data-driven model development, and provide a novel training sample screening approach to achieve high-accuracy prediction under small-sample data conditions.

title: Regional atmospheric pattern shifts associated with weather whiplash events in the upper Yangtze River Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Erya Zhang, Wenhui Li, Shu Chen, Wenquan Gu, Xiaoyan Zhai, Xuezhi Tan
abstract: Global warming and intensified water cycles have led to an increase in weather whiplash events (WWEs), threatening ecosystems and human societies. However, the connection between WWEs and atmospheric circulation dynamics remains poorly understood, particularly through the lens of spatial clustering. This study applies the self-organizing map algorithm to cluster 500 hPa geopotential height (1979–2022) in the upper Yangtze River Basin (UYRB) and identify WWEs based on atmospheric circulation pattern shifts. We evaluate long-term trends in representative atmospheric patterns, extreme events, and WWEs, while exploring their linkages to large-scale circulation backgrounds. Results indicate a significant increase in the frequency of dry-warm patterns and a corresponding decrease in wet-cold patterns, confirming a warming and drying trend in the UYRB. Extreme warm events have risen across all seasons, with increased precipitation volatility in dry-warm patterns. The persistence of dry-warm patterns has also increased, along with a growing number of WWEs originating from dry-warm patterns. These changes are closely linked to dynamic changes in synoptic circulation patterns and moisture transport anomalies.

title: Phenology and snow penman evapotranspiration model: development, validation, and products
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Hongze Cai, Kaicun Wang
abstract: Terrestrial evapotranspiration (ET) regulates land–atmosphere water and energy exchanges, but its estimation remains uncertain. Remote-sensing ET models use satellite-derived land-surface information efficiently, yet many products simplify phenology and snow processes and rely on meteorological inputs that may contain inhomogeneities. Here, we developed a Phenology and Snow Penman (PSP) model to estimate ET and its components by explicitly representing vegetation phenology, snow cover and CO2-induced stomatal inhibition. The model was evaluated using eddy-covariance flux observations from 267 global sites and water-balance ET estimates from 58 basins, and showed comparable performance to widely used ET products. We then drove PSP with the Homogenized Gridded Climate Dataset for China (HCD01) to calculate ET. Including phenology and snow processes improved site-level ET simulation accuracy, while neglecting these processes substantially altered ET magnitude, trends and component partitioning across China. Inhomogeneous meteorological inputs also strongly affected ET estimates, with precipitation and radiation contributing most to these differences. During 2000–2020, vegetation change was the dominant driver of the increasing ET trend over China, whereas CO2-induced stomatal inhibition exerted a small but significant offsetting effect by suppressing transpiration. Driven by homogenized meteorological inputs, PSP estimated a mean annual ET of 434 mm yr−1 over China, with a weak upward trend of 1.45 mm yr−1 dec−1 during 1961–2024. Daily 0.1° ET and component datasets for China are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.11888/Terre.tpdc.303108, including HCD01-driven estimates for 1961–2024 and corresponding estimates with CO2-induced stomatal inhibition for 2000–2020 (Cai and Wang, 2026).

title: Geostatistics-informed latent diffusion for conditional hydrogeological facies simulation under sparse hard-data constraints
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Tianqi Xia, Genshen Chen, Huiyun Mao, Yiping Tian, Zhiting Zhang
abstract: Reconstructing subsurface facies architecture from sparse hard data remains a central challenge in hydrogeological modeling. Although adversarial generative networks have been adopted for conditional facies simulation, they often suffer from mode collapse and local structural discontinuities under stringent hard-data constraints. To address these limitations, we propose a Geostatistics-Informed Latent Diffusion Model (GiLDM) for conditional facies simulation under sparse hard-data constraints. The framework incorporates differentiable geostatistical regularizers into the latent denoising objective, thereby embedding explicit spatial priors throughout the generative process. We further adopt tri-modal training strategy with a stochastic conditioning dropout to reduce deterministic shortcut mappings and improve diversity under strict hard-data conditioning. Evaluation across stationary meandering channels, non-stationary prograding deltas, and multi-facies systems shows that GiLDM maintains high hard-data fidelity, with hard-data hit rates exceeding 99.9% in the meandering-channel and prograding-delta cases. Compared with DS, cGAN, and CMS-SinGAN, GiLDM yields more coherent facies structures and better preserves long-range continuity under sparse hard-data constraints. It also retains same-condition ensemble diversity, with pairwise L1 distances ranging from 0.0606 to 0.109 in both binary cases. Overall, GiLDM generates facies realizations with improved geostatistical consistency and posterior variability, and can serve as a structural prior for subsequent groundwater-flow and contaminant-transport analysis.

title: Evaluating the effectiveness of GSMaP precipitation product in capturing precipitation events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Chun Zhou, Li Zhou, Ting Chen, Juan Du, Jiajia Yue, Keying Liu, Tianqi Ao
abstract: Accurate precipitation monitoring is essential for water resource management and hazard forecasting, yet gauge networks remain sparse and uneven in complex terrain. Using hourly gauge observations from 2004 to 2020, we evaluated the event-scale performance of the Gauge-calibrated Near-Realtime Rainfall Product (GNRT; 0.1°, 1 h) within the Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) across Sichuan Province, China. Our findings reveal the following: (1) precipitation-event characteristics exhibit a pronounced east–west gradient, and GNRT–Gauge biases show clear terrain-related contrasts, with positive depth biases more frequent in the southern dry-hot valley and negative biases in parts of the northeastern humid and western high-elevation regions; (2) GNRT biases vary with event intensity, with light-to-moderate events generally showing shorter durations and spatially heterogeneous depth and mean-rate differences, while heavy and violent events exhibit stronger regional contrasts in duration and peak position; (3) pooled event classifications are dominated by isolated misses and false alarms across all intensity levels. Although station-level event probability of detection is generally higher for heavy and violent events, the event false-alarm ratio remains high and the event critical success index improves only modestly, especially in western mountainous areas; and (4) for matched events, GNRT generally identifies event onset, peak, and cessation earlier than gauges, with the largest negative offsets occurring at event termination. Negative timing offsets are widespread, but their spatial hotspots vary with intensity. These results highlight the need to account for terrain- and intensity-dependent detection and timing errors when using GNRT for precipitation-event monitoring in complex terrain.

title: Determining the trends and drivers of extreme flow in permafrost rivers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Zhiwei Wang, Genxu Wang, Huaiyong Shao, Chunlin Song, Shan Lin, Gang Liu, Zheng Jin, Chen Yu
abstract: Climate warming on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau has altered hydrological processes in permafrost regions, but the contributions of different factors to extreme flows remain unclear, especially at the seasonal scale. Using 50-year daily streamflow data from the Yangtze River source region (YARSR) and the Yellow River source region (YERSR), combined with flow duration curves, statistical correlation analysis, and double mass curves, we quantified the responses of extreme high flow (Q5) and extreme low flow (Q95) to precipitation, temperature, NDVI, and evapotranspiration (ET). The results show that spring Q5 is more sensitive to temperature, NDVI, and ET, while annual, summer, and autumn Q5 are more sensitive to precipitation. Annual Q95 is more sensitive to temperature, and autumn Q95 is more sensitive to precipitation. Temperature exerts a bidirectional influence on extreme flows: it contributes positively to annual Q95 (86.2% in the YARSR) and negatively to spring Q5 (–92.4% in the YARSR, –93.3% in the YERSR). The contribution of precipitation to warm-season extreme floods exceeds 100%, indicating that unquantified negative feedbacks (e.g., ET) partially offset the positive effect of precipitation. NDVI and ET have stronger impacts on spring Q5 than on other extreme flows. The multi-method approach adopted in this study provides a reliable identification of dominant factors for extreme flow changes in alpine permafrost regions, which is of great significance for fully understanding the response mechanisms of extreme flows to climate change and for water resource management in alpine permafrost basins.

title: An integrated framework for characterizing spatiotemporal dynamics of water footprints, water scarcities, water quantity–quality interdependences and coupled risks in a semiarid river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Shuai Liu, Zhiwei Yue, Wei Wang, Xiangkun Zhao, Zhibin Li, La Zhuo
abstract: Reliable assessment of basin-scale water scarcity and its associated risks is critical for ecosystem protection and sustainable development, especially in ecologically fragile semi-arid basins. Nevertheless, the interactions between quantity and quality-induced water scarcities in time and space remain poorly understood, and systematic evaluations of their co-occurrence are still lacking. An integrated framework based on the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), water footprint theory, and Copula functions was developed to characterize and quantify water footprints, water scarcities, water quantity–quality interdependences and coupled risks in the Jing River Basin during 2016–2022. A triple-variable calibration strategy incorporating evapotranspiration, runoff, and water quality was employed to improve the robustness of hydrological and environmental simulations. Results showed clear spatiotemporal differences among water scarcity types. Green water scarcity (GWS) mainly occurred during the crop growing season (May–October), whereas blue water scarcity (BWS) was concentrated in the dry season (November–April). In contrast, quality-induced water scarcity (QWS) showed weak seasonality and stronger control by local conditions. Severe water scarcity (BWS–GWS–QWS) was rare but clustered in localized hotspots, persisting for 5–6 months annually. Joint distribution analysis showed that the interdependence between water quantity and quality was dominated by Gumbel and Clayton Copulas in 75% of sub-basins, indicating potential asymmetric dependence patterns under the available 7-year monthly record. Meanwhile, low-flow conditions were more often associated with elevated QWS, and higher joint risk probabilities were observed in some agriculturally dominated sub-basins. This integrated approach helps constrain SWAT-based simulations and characterizes the non-linear dependence between water quantity and quality across varying hydrological scenarios. Ultimately, this study supports a transition toward coupled quantity-quality management, providing actionable intelligence for spatially targeted agricultural interventions, such as non-point source pollution control, and crop structure adjustments, to enhance resilience against multiple water scarcities in semi-arid river basins.

title: Isotope-informed assessment of groundwater nitrate attenuation and N 2 O-related risk in contrasting river-network lowlands
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Shenhao Qu, Dongli She, Weilian Chen, Junhan Zhao, Li Zhang, Peng Chen, Yongchun Pan, Yongqiu Xia
abstract: Shallow aquifers in agricultural river-network lowlands receive sustained diffuse nitrate inputs. Drainage connectivity and hydraulic regulation continually reorganize groundwater recharge, mixing, and redox conditions. Consequently, nitrate attenuation and associated nitrous oxide (N2O) risk vary markedly across space and time, yet their coupled patterns remain poorly constrained. We integrated stable water isotopes (δ2H–H2O, δ18O–H2O), line-conditioned excess (lc-excess), excess N2 (eN2), dissolved N2O (dN2O), nitrate removal efficiency (RE), and an EF5g-based groundwater N2O risk indicator (EF5g). We compared the engineered, pump-regulated Changshu polder with the naturally connected Haining ditch-corridor system. Their nearly non-overlapping monitoring periods covered broadly comparable seasonal hydro-meteorological gradients and were treated as a type-based comparison. Groundwater in both systems largely retained meteoric recharge signatures. Changshu showed stronger month-to-month shifts and greater among-well dispersion in lc-excess, whereas Haining remained comparatively stable after early fluctuations. eN2 varied relatively smoothly, with a pronounced summer minimum in Changshu and broader increases during late summer–autumn in Haining. In contrast, dN2O showed sharper fluctuations and stronger upper-tail behavior, particularly in Haining. Lower RE and elevated EF5g partially overlapped during the warm season in Changshu, while Haining exhibited greater among-well heterogeneity and more persistent high-end EF5g observations. Central EF5g values in both systems remained below the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 2006 default of 0.0025, but maxima reached 0.0037 in Changshu and 0.0039 in Haining. Partial least squares regression explained substantial RE variability ( Q cum 2 = 0.685 and 0.543, respectively) and identified NO3 –-N, dissolved oxygen, and electrical conductivity as the leading predictors in both systems. The greater contribution of lc-excess in the engineered Changshu polder highlighted the value of isotope-recorded recharge, exchange, and mixing histories under frequently reorganized hydrological states. EF5g was poorly predicted by the same monthly variables, indicating greater sensitivity to fine-scale redox heterogeneity and transient N2O production–reduction imbalances. This integrated framework supports process-based assessment of groundwater nitrate attenuation and N2O risk in river-network lowlands.

title: Spatial attribution analysis of river water quality by integrating remote sensing inversion and multi-source land cover data: An interpretable topological residual Knowledge-Driven Graph Attention Network (ITRK-GAT)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Xiaonan Yang, Peixiong He, Yang Zhang, Yong Bao, Hongyan Zhang, Jiansheng Wang, Li Sun, Songjia Zhang, Yong Liu, Qingli Li
abstract: Accelerating urbanization places urban river networks under intense, spatially heterogeneous human pressure; yet conventional remote-sensing inversion, though effective for large-scale monitoring, reveals little about pollution sources, transport pathways, or their terrestrial mechanisms. To help bridge this “inversion-over-attribution” gap, this study proposes an interpretable Topological Residual Knowledge-Driven Graph Attention Network (ITRK-GAT), for the Lianqi River, Shanghai. The framework couples multi-source terrestrial features—land use, discharge outfalls, and pollution-related enterprises—with river-network topology through an undirected graph over river grid units, in which topological relationships and along-stream distance priors act as structural constraints for physically consistent propagation. Chemical oxygen demand (COD) is predicted with accuracy outperforming standard graph and tabular baselines, and ablation confirms the contribution of each module. Integrated Gradients attribution and attention mapping jointly indicate that residential and industrial land use, together with discharge outfalls, are most strongly associated with elevated COD, with high-attribution regions co-located with tributary confluences and discharge-dense corridors. Controlled perturbation further shows that these associations propagate along network connectivity and attenuate with topological distance, while the attribution ranking stays stable under inversion-induced label noise. Together, these analyses establish a robust, physically coherent attribution framework offering an interpretable and transferable basis for pollution-source tracing and spatially differentiated management of urban rivers.

title: Validation of GRACE, ERA5-Land and MODIS remote sensing products for groundwater monitoring in semiarid regions: A multi-basin study in Chile’s Coquimbo region
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Francisco Parra, Juan Fernando Rubilar
abstract: Groundwater monitoring in semiarid regions faces significant challenges due to sparse and expensive in-situ networks. We evaluate GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage, ERA5-Land precipitation, and MODIS vegetation indices against 56 years (1970-2025) of depth-to-water-table measurements from 121 wells in Chile’s semiarid Coquimbo Region, spanning nine basins of which eight contain monitoring wells. Because depth to water is measured positive downward, wetter conditions correspond to negative correlations with storage products. Annual aggregation strengthens correlations relative to monthly analysis (GRACE: r=−0.17 to r=−0.56), but effective-sample-size corrections and first-difference analysis show that these correlations reflect a shared decadal drying trajectory rather than interannual coupling: year-to-year changes in depth to water are uncorrelated with GRACE. Formal trend analysis (Mann-Kendall with autocorrelation correction) establishes the trajectory-level agreement: before the 2010–2021 megadrought, depth to water (+0.34 m/yr) and JPL TWS (−0.96 cm/yr) show significant parallel trends. During the megadrought they decouple completely: depth to water deepens at + 0.50 m/yr (p = 0.0005) while none of three mascon solutions (JPL, CSR, GSFC) detects a storage trend. Multi-solution comparison further shows that the local GRACE signal is solution-dependent at this scale (inter-solution r = 0.36-0.54), with JPL redistributing an Andean-centered signal over the coastal basins. Error propagation shows the GLDAS-based groundwater separation is uncertainty-dominated (sigma of the same order as the signal). ERA5-Land precipitation shows no zero-lag association with depth to water, but a robust 1-year-lagged response (r=−0.38, p = 0.004, n = 55) that survives all statistical corrections — the only interannual coupling detected. Satellite gravimetry can corroborate regional decadal drying trajectories where dense well networks exist, but cannot substitute in-situ monitoring at the basin scale: it misses interannual variability and, critically, extraction-driven depletion. All scripts are available via GitHub.

title: Rapid hydrologic flushing and biogeochemical recovery after Hurricane Helene in a heterogeneous coastal karst system
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Dini Adyasari, Xiaolang Zhang, Adelide Rianda, Karl Kaiser, Bohyun Yeo
abstract: Extreme storms can substantially alter hydrologic and biogeochemical processes in coastal systems, yet the coupled responses of surface water and groundwater, particularly within karst terrains, remain poorly understood. This study integrated continuous United States Geological Survey (USGS) monitoring with multi-compartment water sampling conducted between October 2024 and May 2025 to evaluate coastal system responses to Hurricane Helene, which made landfall along Florida’s Big Bend coast in September 2024. The regional karstic Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA), together with the connected Wakulla Spring–Wakulla River system, responded rapidly to the hurricane, with river, spring, and groundwater stages increasing to approximately 3, 1.5, and 1.1 times their respective baseflow levels within hours of landfall. USGS monitoring records indicate that the Wakulla River, Wakulla Spring, and regional UFA system returned to near-baseflow conditions within approximately 14 days, 23 days, and 3 months after landfall, respectively. These recovery trends were further supported by stable water isotope signatures and nutrient dynamics. River and spring conductivity time series and major ion patterns suggest minimal storm-surge-driven salinization throughout the study area. In contrast, shallow porous groundwater responses varied among hydrogeologic compartments. Sites located closest to the river exhibited recovery trajectories similar to those of surface waters, likely reflecting stronger hydrologic connectivity. More isolated shallow groundwater systems showed slower and more variable biogeochemical recovery, with ammonia and phosphate concentrations continuing to increase more than eight months after the hurricane, indicating prolonged biogeochemical processing within coastal sediments. Overall, the regional karstic system recovered more rapidly than many previously reported storm-affected coastal systems, likely due to the high transmissivity of the karst conduit network and the rapid inland progression of Hurricane Helene. The contrasting responses among hydrologic compartments demonstrate that conduit-dominated aquifers can rapidly flush storm-derived waters while still sustaining localized and persistent biogeochemical disturbances within shallow coastal sediments. These findings further suggest that future hydrologic and reactive transport models should incorporate multiple groundwater endmembers and vertical aquifer heterogeneity to better predict water quality responses to increasingly frequent extreme events.

title: Reshaped hydrologic controls on groundwater chemistry in coal‑mining critical zones: a transition from mining dominance to agricultural nutrient inputs
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Wenxu Hu, Yong Xiao, Yuqing Zhang, Qiulan Zhang, Jiahua Wei, Qichen Hao, Yanlong Li, Junting Liu, Jie Wang, Liwei Wang, Zikun Ma
abstract: Coal extraction is widely recognized as the predominant anthropogenic modulator of groundwater hydrochemistry in intensely exploited coalfields. However, the mechanisms by which fully mechanized longwall mining reshapes groundwater hydrochemical evolution remain inadequately understood. This research takes a representative coalfield of the Ordos Basin in China as a case to explore the hydrochemical features and dominant control mechanisms of groundwater in coal‑mining critical zones, via the integration of cluster analysis, quantitative source apportionment, and explainable artificial intelligence techniques. Results reveal pronounced hydrochemical heterogeneity within phreatic aquifers. Groundwater is classified into six distinct groups, with hydrochemical facies evolving from HCO3-Ca type to saline types enriched in NO3 –, Cl-, and SO4 2-. Groundwater chemistry is primarily controlled by natural water–rock interactions, with secondary anthropogenic alterations. Quantitative source apportionment reveals that agricultural activities constitute the largest anthropogenic input (20.4%), slightly exceeding the contributions from coal mine drainage mixing (18.3%). The XGBoost model achieves reliable prediction performance for groundwater quality suitability (R2 = 0.80), and SHAP analysis identifies NO3 –, Fe, SO4 2-, and TDS as key indicators governing water quality variations. Agricultural activities substantially affect groundwater quality by driving nitrate accumulation and salt migration via irrigation return flow and nutrient leaching. Under current mechanized longwall mining and mine-water management schemes, mining-induced hydrogeological disturbances are effectively limited. In contrast, near-surface agricultural nutrient inputs have emerged as the dominant anthropogenic control on phreatic groundwater quality. These findings highlight a shift in hydrologic controls across coal-mining critical zones under modern mining practices and provide scientific support for adaptive groundwater management.

title: Analyzing the resilience and development trajectories of water resource systems in transboundary river basins: Lessons from the Mekong
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Lin Chai, Liang Yuan, Weijun He, Dagmawi Mulugeta Degefu, Xia Wu, Yang Kong, Thomas Stephen Ramsey
abstract: Assessing the resilience of water resource systems is fundamental to sustainable risk management in transboundary river basins. With the increasing frequency of extreme weather events and rising water demand, risks in transboundary river basins have become more pronounced. This study examines the dynamics of Water Resources System Resilience (WRSR) in the Mekong River Basin (MRB) and identifies key obstacles affecting its enhancement. A resilience framework comprising perception, resistance, recovery, and adaptive abilities was used to construct the WRSR evaluation index. Indicator weights were determined using the entropy method, and system resilience was evaluated through the five–element connection model. The subtraction set pair potential model and Mann-Kendall trend analysis were applied to assess temporal evolution, while the obstacle degree model was used to diagnose major barriers to sustainable water governance. Results indicate that from 1995 to 2020, WRSR in the MRB remained predominantly at a low level. Among the riparian states, China consistently maintained high resilience; Cambodia experienced steady improvement; and Laos and Thailand remained at a moderate level. In contrast, Myanmar and Vietnam showed persistently low resilience. The priority areas for resilience enhancement vary across countries: Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar need to strengthen their resistance capacity; China and Thailand should further develop both perception and resistance capacities; whereas Vietnam requires simultaneous improvements in perception, disaster resistance, and adaptive capacities. Fertilizer use per unit area, industrial water use efficiency, total internal renewable water resources per capita, GDP per capita, and dam capacity per capita constitute the principal obstacles to WRSR, with resistance capacity emerging as a dominant critical limiting factor.

title: Ecological water replenishment improves water quality and environmental capacity in a tributary of the Yellow River: insights from MIKE 21 coupled modeling
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yihao Wen, Junzheng Liu, Haijue Xu, Jinliang Zhang, Yuchuan Bai, Yao Wang
abstract: Water quality deterioration in seasonally water-scarce rivers poses a persistent challenge to water-quality and water-resource management. Ecological water replenishment (EWR) is increasingly used as a hydrological regulation measure, but quantitative evidence remains limited regarding how alternative EWR scenarios affect modeled water quality and water environmental capacity. This study developed a coupled hydrodynamic–water quality model based on MIKE 21 for the Yi River — a key tributary of the Yellow River Basin — to quantify the simulated spatiotemporal responses of six water quality parameters and reach-scale water environmental capacity to prescribed EWR scenarios. Six scenarios were simulated, comprising three non-replenishment scenarios (wet, normal, and dry hydrological years) and three replenishment strategies (varying discharge intensity and duration) applied under the critical dry-year hydrodynamic condition with a prescribed Class IV in-channel baseline and Class II replenishment inflow. The model demonstrated acceptable performance across six water quality parameters (DO, BOD5, CODMn, COD, NH3-N, and TP), with Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency coefficients ≥ 0.777 and maximum MAPE of 13.76%. Non-replenishment simulations revealed that pollutant concentrations were consistently highest in the upstream reach and most severe during the dry year, when upstream COD and NH3-N were classified as Class IV in some months. Under this setting, high-discharge, short-duration replenishment (2Q, T/2) produced the greatest modeled water-quality improvement among the tested equal-volume constant-discharge scenarios, reducing the comprehensive pollution index from 0.726 to 0.360 and achieving a 227.33% increase in downstream DO (from 3.0 mg/L, Class IV, to 9.82 mg/L, Class II) and a 91.17% reduction in BOD5 (from 6.0 mg/L, Class IV, to 0.53 mg/L, Class II). Under the adopted Class III target and reach-scale capacity formulation, the modeled total water environmental capacity after EWR was 33.6% higher than that before EWR, with the largest absolute increase estimated for CODMn. These findings provide a quantitative framework for comparing water-quality-oriented EWR scenarios and identifying pollution-control priorities during low-flow periods.

title: Enhanced simulations of overland-gully-sewer flow interactions in coupled three-layer dual drainage modeling
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Chia-Ho Wang, Hsiang-Lin Yu, Tsang-Jung Chang, Albert S. Chen
abstract: This study presents an enhanced approach for efficient and accurate simulations of overland-gully-sewer (2D-1D-1D) urban inundation modeling for highly urbanized areas with gully networks. The current 2D-1D-1D urban inundation modeling is a three-layer dual drainage model that comprises a 2D overland flow model (2D-OFM), a 1D gully flow model (1D-GFM), a 1D sewer flow model (1D-SFM), and dynamic interactions among them. Despite its favorable performance, its applicability remains limited as its 1D-GFM requires substantial detailed local drainage (gully) data to build and maintain. Also, 1D-GFM simulates gully flows by an iterative process such that the overall efficiency is constrained when heavy computational demands are introduced by excessive gullies and gully inlets. In view of this, a novel 1D virtual gully flow model (1D-VGFM) is proposed to replace 1D-GFM. It requires less detailed drainage data to build and can simulate gully flows using simple algebraic equations. Based on results from three historical flood events, the present approach maintains accuracy comparable to that of the selected conventional approach, while significantly reducing the data complexity for gully system representation from 11 to 3 and achieving a satisfactory acceleration of up to 42.5%. As a result, it is proven to be a useful alternative for urban inundation modeling.

title: Molecular-level source contribution of dissolved organic matter in a typical plateau lake using end-member mixing analysis based on spectroscopic, stable isotope and molecular fingerprint
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yunxuan Cheng, Shasha Liu, Rui Fu, Yi Ren, Yuxuan Zhang, Ziwen Yin, Fengchang Wu
abstract: Lakes receive and actively process dissolved organic matter (DOM) from diverse sources, thereby influencing water quality and the global carbon cycle. Accurately identifying DOM sources and apportioning their relative contributions are critical for effective lake management and understanding carbon cycling in lacustrine ecosystems. However, precise source attribution remains challenging because DOM originates from heterogeneous sources and undergoes continuous biogeochemical transformations. Here, we quantified DOM source contributions in Erhai Lake, a typical plateau lake, using end-member mixing analysis based on stable isotope, spectroscopic, and molecular fingerprint data. The results indicated that wet season DOM exhibited stronger optical signatures of humification and aromaticity, greater molecular unsaturation, a higher oxidation state, and enrichment in nitrogen- and sulfur-containing formulas, whereas dry season DOM was more reduced and enriched in CHO formulas. Analysis of the potential DOM end-members showed that anthropogenic inputs, including manure and wastewater treatment plant effluent, were less humified and less unsaturated than natural watershed sources such as forest soil and riverine inputs, but more oxygenated than most internal lake sources, such as algae and bottom sediments. Comparison of lake and end-member DOM identified common relatively recalcitrant formulas, from which retained molecular markers were selected according to source specificity. Random forest analysis was then used to select indicative parameters of these markers for incorporation into the end-member mixing models. Based on convergence diagnostics and posterior credible intervals, the model incorporating stable isotope, optical, and molecular data was identified as optimal and was subsequently used to quantify DOM sources in Erhai Lake. The model results showed that anthropogenic inputs made the largest contribution in both seasons, accounting for 44.61% in the dry season and 42.63% in the wet season. Natural watershed sources contributed 29.24% and 26.54% of the DOM pool during the dry and wet seasons, respectively, whereas internal lake sources accounted for 26.15% and 30.83%, respectively. Manure was the largest individual source in the dry season (34.03%), whereas agricultural runoff was the largest individual source in the wet season (15.93%). This framework provides a molecularly constrained approach for DOM source apportionment and highlights hydrological control over seasonal source structure in Erhai Lake.

title: A new breakthrough pressure model for coal considering effective stress and water saturation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Tiancheng Zhang, Jimmy Xuekai Li, Luwei Ding, Dan Kuznetsov, Victor Rudolph, Zhongwei Chen
abstract: Gas breakthrough pressure is a key parameter governing gas migration in reservoirs and plays a critical role in assessing the safety of geological storage of gases such as CO2 and H2. However, existing breakthrough pressure prediction methods largely rely on empirical correlations fitted to experimental data, which lack a solid physical basis and are unable to simultaneously account for the coupled effects of water saturation and effective stress. In this study, a series of gas breakthrough pressure experiments were conducted on coal samples from Bowen Basin under varying effective stress and water saturation conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that cleat networks, effective stress, and water saturation jointly control breakthrough behavior in coal reservoirs. Based on these observations, a new physics–informed gas breakthrough pressure model for coal was developed by incorporating effective stress, water saturation, cleat compressibility, porosity, and initial permeability within a unified theoretical framework. The proposed model enables direct prediction of breakthrough pressure curves using sample-specific physical parameters and improves prediction accuracy compared with existing models, particularly for low-permeability samples. Compared with the J-function and the exponential model, it reduces the overall mean absolute error across the five samples from 36.8 kPa and 18.7 kPa to 12.1 kPa, corresponding to reductions of 67.1% and 35.3%, respectively. This study provides a robust approach for predicting gas breakthrough pressure in coal reservoirs and offers insights into underground gas storage assessment.

title: Estimating drain spacing in non-steady state drainage with constant recharge
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Leonidas Mindrinos, George Kargas
abstract: The paper presents a numerical solution for determining the spacing of subsurface drainage systems under unsteady drainage conditions, when a constant recharge rate ( R ) is incorporated into the linearized Boussinesq equation under specified boundary and initial conditions. To date, the exponential-series solution of the Boussinesq equation has been used to compute the water table elevation at the midpoint (m) between parallel drains, as well as the discharge per unit area into the drains (q), but not for determining the drain spacing ( L ) , since L appears both algebraically and within the exponential term. To address this issue, only the first term of the exponential series was used. The results indicate that the proposed numerical solution, together with necessary conditions guaranteeing solvability and convergence, provides reliable estimates of L over a wide range of hydraulic and design parameters. The largest errors are obtained when the hydraulic conductivity (K) and drainable porosity (S) are varied, with RMSE values of 0.33 m and 0.36 m, respectively, followed by variations in the observation time (t) (RMSE = 0.20 m). In contrast, variations in R and drain depth (D) result in considerably smaller errors, with RMSE values of 0.06 m and 0.09 m, respectively. Overall, the proposed scheme provides reliable and stable (with respect to measurement noise) estimates of drain spacing and can be effectively applied to the design of subsurface drainage systems.

title: Anomalously depleted δ 2 H signatures of tropical cyclone precipitation recorded in tree-ring lignin methoxy groups
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Yabo Wang, Wenxin Li, Xiaohong Liu, Guobao Xu, Huhu Kang, Bingming Chen, Xianhui Tang, Jianjun Qu, Chong Jiang, Xin Song
abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most destructive weather systems in the Earth system, yet their long-term variability remains poorly constrained because instrumental observations and historical archives span only the recent decades. Terrestrial proxies capable of preserving cyclone-related hydroclimatic signals could therefore provide valuable insights into past TC activity. However, whether and how TC signals are quantitatively preserved in tree-ring hydrogen isotopes remains largely unresolved. Here we investigate the isotopic imprint of TCs in both precipitation and tree rings in the Hong Kong SAR, China. By compiling TC events since 1980 and comparing the hydrogen isotopic composition of precipitation (δ2Hppt) during TC-affected and TC-free months, we show that TC precipitation (TCP) consistently exhibits anomalously depleted isotopic signatures even after accounting for rainfall amount and seasonal effects. Because precipitation isotopes provide the primary hydrogen source incorporated into plant water pools and subsequently into lignin methoxy groups during wood formation, these isotopic anomalies are expected to propagate into tree-ring hydrogen isotopes. Consistent with this mechanism, robust regression analyses indicate that TCP isotopic variability explains approximately 30% of the variance in latewood lignin methoxy hydrogen isotopes (δ2HLM) of Pinus elliottii Engelm. in Hong Kong. We further find that TCP exerts the dominant influence on δ2HLM variability, with additional contributions from storm intensity and seasonal timing, whereas storm duration and cyclone–site distance show limited independent effects. These results indicate that TC signals preserved in latewood δ2HLM reflect the integrated hydroclimatic influence of cyclone systems rather than any single storm metric. Together, our findings demonstrate that TC-driven hydro-isotopic anomalies can be transmitted from precipitation to tree-ring latewood δ2HLM and preserved within terrestrial archives. These results highlight the potential of tree-ring δ2HLM as a complementary archive for investigating past TC-related hydroclimatic variability and provide a basis for extending records of TC activity beyond the instrumental period.

title: Influence of emergent and submerged plants on local hydrodynamics and turbulence anisotropy in vegetated rivers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part B Author(s): Giuseppe Francesco Cesare Lama, Andrea Del Gaudio, Jyotirmoy Barman, Anurag Handique, Francesco De Paola, Giovanni Battista Chirico, Donatella Termini
abstract: This study investigates the influence of three plants configurations – Full emergent Vegetation (FV), Central Cut (CC), and Extensive Cut (EC) – on the hydrodynamics and turbulence anisotropy within a reclamation channel colonized by rigid Phragmites australis plants. Turbulence anisotropy is quantified via both turbulence intensities and anisotropy invariant map (AIM) derived from the Reynolds stress deviatoric tensor. Results demonstrate that FV setup induces the highest anisotropy, characterized by a quasi-two-component (disk-like) turbulence regime due to enhanced horizontal fluctuations. Conversely, EC and CC configurations promote vertical fluctuations and near-bed oblate (disk-like, from three- to two-component) turbulence with transition to prolate (rod-like, from three- to one-component) anisotropy tendencies near the free surface. In the CC configuration, the side emergent uncut plants stands foster lateral velocity gradients and transverse momentum exchange. These results demonstrate how plants spatial distribution and submergence modulate local turbulence anisotropy and hydrodynamics governing vegetated watercourses.

title: Optimal reservoir flood-control operation under successive rainfall events during the Meiyu season
description: Publication date: Available online 31 August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Yuchang Mo, Yunfei Li, Shuaisen Ma, Qingan Qiu, Rui Peng
abstract: Reservoir flood-control operation during the Meiyu season is challenged by successive rainfall events, compound flood-wave superposition, and the conflicting objectives of flood safety and operational economy. Existing studies often represent rainfall uncertainty through independent events or aggregated inflow scenarios, which may overlook the temporal clustering and self-exciting characteristics of successive Meiyu rainfall events. This work develops a dynamic staged spillway-operation framework for reservoir flood-control scheduling under clustered rainfall conditions. A marked Hawkes process is employed to characterize the stochastic occurrence and temporal dependence of successive rainfall events, while a duration-corrected Gamma response kernel is introduced to describe the runoff generation and superposition process. Based on these components, a threshold-driven scheduling model is established, in which spillway operation levels are adaptively adjusted according to the real-time conditional non-failure probability. The optimal threshold structure is obtained by minimizing the expected operating cost through a nested Monte Carlo simulation framework coupled with particle swarm optimization. A case study of the Xin’anjiang Reservoir demonstrates that the proposed framework provides a better balance between flood-control reliability and operational cost compared with empirical, conservative, and aggressive scheduling strategies. Further analyses reveal that rainfall clustering characteristics, runoff-response parameters, and initial reservoir storage conditions significantly influence the optimal operation strategy. The proposed framework offers a risk-responsive and cost-aware approach for reservoir flood-control operation under successive rainfall events during the Meiyu season.

title: Coastal aquifer vulnerability to salinization under sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction pressure in a Mediterranean karst system
description: Publication date: Available online 31 August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): R. Álvarez Alonso, P.A. Robledo Ardila, C.A. Melo Aguilar, J.J. Durán Valsero, R. Morales, S. Martínez Pérez
abstract: Sea-level rise and groundwater abstraction are reshaping coastal systems in karst environments, particularly in low-gradient coastal plains where groundwater-dependent ecosystems are strongly coupled to aquifer dynamics. However, most coastal assessments remain based on topographic inundation and shoreline retreat, neglecting groundwater processes that influence the inland propagation of marine influence. This study presents a GIS-based hydro-coastal vulnerability screening framework designed to identify areas potentially influenced by the combined effects of sea-level rise and groundwater stress. The approach integrates (i) DEM-based potential marine inundation, (ii) hydrogeological signals of piezometric decline and salinization derived from monitoring data, and (iii) a multi-criteria hydro-coastal vulnerability index incorporating ecological sensitivity, hydrogeological susceptibility, anthropogenic pressure, and system resilience. Direct potential marine inundation alone affects between 9.24 and 43.76 km2 (0.25–1.20% of the island) across sea level rise scenarios but underestimates the inland extent of coastal influence. Including groundwater indicators identifies a broader scenario-based coastal influence zone and increases ecosystem exposure, with up to 97% of wetland area potentially exposed within the integrated coastal-influence zone under high-end scenarios. Vulnerability is concentrated in low-lying coastal plains, particularly in s’Albufera, Campos–Es Trenc, and Albufereta, where strong aquifer–sea connectivity and anthropogenic pressure converge. These findings suggest that coastal evolution in Mediterranean karst settings emerges from the interaction between surface and groundwater processes and highlight that hydrogeologically informed regional screening approaches may identify coastal areas extending beyond static representations of the MTPD, thereby informing future coastal-domain management rather than redefining regulatory boundaries.

title: Integration of vertical and lateral erosion in modelling landslide mass flows, debris flows and flash floods
description: Publication date: Available online 31 August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Ruochen Jiang, Wenjun Lu, Shihao Xiao, Xin He, Ruiqiang Bai, Yingyue Han, Mingdong Wei, Dalei Peng, Jian He, Limin Zhang
abstract: Overtopping and lateral erosion play a critical role in geomorphological evolution due to landslides, debris flows, fluvial floods and dam-breaching floods. These processes contribute substantial materials to runoff channels, significantly amplifying the flow volume and destructive power. Existing physics-based models suffer from oversimplified flow dynamics (e.g., constant flow properties or 1D approaches that ignore lateral erosion) or high computational costs (e.g., full 3D fluid dynamics simulations), limiting their accuracy and applications. To address these limitations, this study presents a novel depth-averaged numerical framework that simultaneously captures overtopping and lateral erosion dynamics. Beyond simulating these key erosional mechanisms, the model uniquely incorporates dynamic feedback between erosion processes and evolving properties of the flowing mass. The model performance is demonstrated through rigorous validation across three benchmark cases: (1) controlled dam-breaching experiments, (2) the 2020 Zelunglung landslide-debris flow cascade, and (3) the 2018 Sedongpu outburst flood.
