New hydrological insights for the region Three ES response types emerge: decreasing (water conveyance), single-peaked (aesthetics, recreation), and increasing, with the latter further divided into threshold-triggered or saturating (e.g., flood mitigation, navigation) and continuous growth (e.g., water supply, nutrient cycling) subtypes. Heterogeneous responses form four synergistic bundles and two key trade-offs (sociohydrological vs. eco-hydrological bundles; downstream vs. local services). The models capture four distinct seasonal patterns of ES, reflecting differential flow dependency. Long-term simulations (1950–2013) show that while regulated flows stabilize overall service potentials, they also increase vulnerabilities in flow pulse-dependent supporting services, such as floodplain habitats and carbon storage, which rely on natural flow variability. Annual average ES potential correlates strongly with runoff via power-law, quadratic, or logarithmic functions, enabling predictions of service shifts under hydroclimatic change. This transferable framework supports adaptive water resource management by enabling scenario-based assessment of trade-offs between ecological integrity and human well-being.

title: Wetlands' e-hydroperiod method: Frequency-of-occurrence-based approach
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Sofía Álvarez-Castrejón, Sergio A. Salinas-Rodríguez, Roberto Rodríguez Bastarmérito, Delma Nataly Castelblanco-Martínez, Alejandro Ortega-Argueta, Rodimiro Ramos Reyes
abstract: Study region the Great Lagoon of Catazajá is a Ramsar site and habitat for the Greater Caribbean manatee (Trichechus manatus manatus). It is located in the floodplain of the Usumacinta River, the mightiest river in Mesoamerica, and a transboundary basin with most of its course running through western Guatemala and southern Mexico. Study focus This study aims to present a methodological approach for the evaluation of the environmental water allocation specific for the wetlands (e-hydroperiod) with the theoretical principles of eflows. The low-volumes are parametrised separately from the peak-events, and the frequency of occurrence at which the hydrological conditions and types of peak events are integrated based on the environmental objective selected from a four-to-five-tier class system. The research in Mexico serves as a proof-of-concept and as a fitness evaluation for the model. The results reveal an overall good level of the method’s performance against the natural regime (R2 ≥ 0.93). New hydrological insight This study addresses the limited availability of wetlands-dedicated frameworks to allocate water for environmental processes that contemplate wetlands’ hydrological dynamics. Frequency-based e-hydroperiod components support the Freshwater Challenge goal of restoring 350 million ha of wetlands by 2030, and its implementation secures water for both sustainable use and ecological functions.

title: Integrating ecosystem service assessment and zoning management for transboundary environmental protection: A case study of the China–Vietnam Beilun river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Kai Jiang, Bin Wu, Wenzhu Zhang, Xuan Zhong, Shengquan Lu, Rucheng Lu
abstract: Study region The China–Vietnam Beilun River Cross-Border Basin (BRCB). Study focus Transboundary basins are ecologically sensitive areas with major management challenges between countries, yet assessments of asymmetric ecological conditions and transboundary zoning remain limited. Taking the BRCB as the study area, this study developed an integrated ecosystem service assessment framework by combining InVEST,GWR, OPGD, hotspot analysis, and SOM. It systematically evaluated the dynamics of five ecosystem services (ESs), their trade-offs and synergies, and explored optimization schemes for transboundary zoning. New hydrological insights Over the past two decades, only water yield (WY) and soil conservation (SC) improved in the BRCB, with better performance on the Chinese side. ES hotspots were concentrated in northwestern forestlands on the Chinese side, while coldspots mainly occurred in southeastern transboundary built-up areas; multifunctional hotspots declined over time. OPGD results showed that ESs were mainly controlled by natural geographical factors, while socioeconomic influences strengthened, highlighting human impacts. Ecosystem service bundles (ESBs) differed markedly across the border: SC bundles and core ES bundles expanded on the Chinese side, whereas the Vietnamese side remained relatively stable. The study reveals country-level ecological imbalance in the BRCB and stresses the need for transnational monitoring and zoning management to support ecological sustainability in transboundary basins.

title: Topographic water redistribution, rather thanclimate, dictates eco-hydrological recovery: Flux- and runoff-based validation in the Upper Minjiang River, eastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yong Liu, Ran Li, Liangshuai Wei, Anbang Huang, Qinfeng Shu, Xin Zhang
abstract: Study region The upper Minjiang River, a 22,954 km² alpine-gorge headwater basin on the eastern margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and a critical water conservation area for the Yangtze River. Study focus Large-scale greening is widely reported across mountain headwaters, yet optical indices demonstrate only that a basin has become greener—not that its water cycle has been physically restructured. This study integrates a 39-year (1986–2024) Landsat-derived Remote Sensing Ecological Index (RSEI) series, GeoDetector-based spatial attribution, MODIS evapotranspiration (ET) fluxes, and 33 years of in-situ discharge records to determine what dictates the spatial pattern of ecological recovery and whether that recovery has genuinely enhanced watershed hydrological regulation. New hydrological insights for the region Eco-hydrological quality declined to a historical nadir in 1997 and then recovered rapidly through 2024 (Sen's slope = 0.0027 yr⁻¹, p 0.05)—indicating that macro-climatic amelioration alone cannot explain the reversal. Elevation dominated the spatial attribution (q = 0.14), roughly sevenfold that of precipitation (q = 0.02), and their pronounced non-linear interaction (DEM∩P, q = 0.194) revealed a “topographic amplifier” whereby rugged terrain intercepts, stratifies, and laterally redistributes an otherwise uniform climatic input, thereby dictating where recovery materializes. Recovery proved hydrologically heterogeneous: arid valleys (< 2000 m) greened most strongly but at the steepest water cost (ET trend = 2.40 mm yr⁻¹); the subalpine belt regenerated most water-efficiently (1.33 mm yr⁻¹); and the nival zone showed rising ET al.ongside declining RSEI, signaling warming-driven rather than restorative wetting. Basin-wide ET rose significantly (trend = 1.458 mm yr⁻¹) and the inter-annual runoff coefficient fell from 0.79 to 0.74, yet the dry-season baseflow contribution increased from 20.16% to 25.02%—two expressions of a single “ecological sponge” effect. Restoration in such basins should therefore be hydrologically constrained rather than area-maximizing.

title: Effects of groundwater level decline on shallow soil water in grassland open-pit mining areas: Water vapor migration and water sources estimation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haibo Feng, Ying Duan, Zhongxia Li, Jianwei Zhou, Yongfeng Gong, Ran Li
abstract: Study region The Chenqi Coalfield in the Hulunbuir grassland, a typical semi-arid grassland open-pit mining area in Inner Mongolia, China, where mining has caused severe groundwater level decline. Study focus This study adopted in situ monitoring and hydrogen-oxygen stable isotope (δD and δ¹⁸O) analysis to clarify the response of shallow (0–100 cm) soil water–vapor–heat dynamics to increasing groundwater level depth (GLD) and to quantify liquid and vapor water sources in the unsaturated zone. New hydrologic insights from the region (1) An integrated isotope-thermodynamic equilibrium method was developed to quantify groundwater contributions to both liquid and vapor water in shallow soils. (2) With rising GLD, the minimum relative humidity (RH) in the surface layer decreased from 67.8% to 20.5%, weakening groundwater's temperature regulation capacity and expanding the active temperature layer from 40 cm to 100 cm depth. (3) Deeper GLDs reduced the frequency and depth range of condensation-favorable conditions, with potential implications for root-zone water availability. (4) When GLD < 4 m, groundwater-derived liquid water averaged 227.13 ± 14.95 kg/m³ and vapor water averaged 0.76 ± 0.06 g/m³ , approximately twice the values under deeper GLD conditions. The results provide a site-specific hydrological threshold and a transferable methodological framework for groundwater management and ecological restoration in grassland mining areas.

title: MODFLOW-informed machine learning for interpretable groundwater level prediction under sparse monitoring conditions in the Eastern Mitidja Aquifer, Northern Algeria
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Fatima Kastali, Mohamed Meddi, Abdelmadjid Boufekane, Ousmane Seidou
abstract: Predicting groundwater levels in semi-arid regions is challenging because groundwater systems are controlled by complex processes and monitoring data are often scarce. This study compares six machine learning models—Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, LightGBM, RBF-SVR, LSTM, and CNN—for groundwater level prediction in the El Hamiz sub-watershed, northern Algeria. A dataset of 3944 records from 136 monitoring wells (2005–2022) was combined with hydroclimatic variables, satellite-derived indicators, and groundwater abstraction data. Two modelling strategies were evaluated: one trained with observed groundwater levels and another using groundwater heads simulated by a calibrated MODFLOW 6 model during a period with limited observations. The latter was intended to examine whether physically based simulations could support machine learning when groundwater observations were unavailable. RF achieved the best performance (R² = 0.883, NSE = 0.873, RMSE = 2.096 m, KGE = 0.850), followed by XGBoost and LightGBM. The MODFLOW-informed RF also performed well (R² = 0.830; RMSE = 2.320 m), although it did not surpass the observation-based model. A Leave-One-Well-Out analysis using MODFLOW heads as an additional predictor produced a pooled R² of 0.869 and an RMSE of 1.744 m. SHAP analysis identified spatial location, evapotranspiration, groundwater abstraction, and precipitation as the most influential predictors. Prediction intervals showed slight undercoverage, indicating that further uncertainty calibration is needed for groundwater management.

title: Assessing future irrigation demand under climate change and bilateral water sharing in the Mahakali command area
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yogendra Mishra, Erica Shrestha, Tulsi Ram Pokhrel, Aditya Nath Jha, Sudan Ghimire, Shrijana Dhakal
abstract: Study region The Mahakali Irrigation Project (MIP) command area, located in the far-western Terai region of Nepal, relies on transboundary water from the Mahakali River governed by bilateral treaties with India. Study focus This study evaluates the impact of climate change on future crop and irrigation water requirements and assesses whether treaty-based water allocations are sufficient to meet projected demand. Bias-corrected outputs from selected CMIP6 models under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios were used to estimate future climate variables. The FAO CROPWAT model was applied to compute crop water requirement (CWR) and irrigation water requirement (IWR) for near (2026–2050), mid (2051–2075), and far (2076–2100) future periods. New hydrological insights Results reveal a strong seasonal redistribution of water demand driven by warming and shifting precipitation patterns. Irrigation water requirement increases sharply during dry and post-monsoon months, with September showing increases up to 564% and February exceeding 6-fold increases under future scenarios. In contrast, monsoon months (July–August) continue to exhibit negligible irrigation demand due to sufficient rainfall. Despite projected increases in annual precipitation, reductions in early monsoon (June) and post-monsoon (October) rainfall, combined with rising evapotranspiration, lead to significant water deficits during critical crop growth periods. Comparison with treaty-based supply (4.25 m³/s in dry season and 28.35 m³/s in wet season) indicates that future irrigation demand may exceed available supply by up to 30–40 m³ /s during dry months, highlighting a substantial seasonal mismatch. These findings demonstrate that timing of water availability, rather than total annual volume, is the dominant control on future irrigation stress, emphasizing the need for adaptive water allocation, storage expansion, and climate-resilient irrigation planning in transboundary river systems.

title: Response of water resources in Jialing River Basin to environmental changes using a remote sensing enhanced hydrological model
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Shanhu Jiang, Mingyan Wu, Fuquan Ni, Liliang Ren, Menghao Wang, Hao Cui, Xinyu Gao, Moran Xu
abstract: Study region Jialing River Basin of southwest China. Study focus Climate change exacerbates the imbalance in water-resource allocation, while land-surface conditions strongly regulate water resources across different spatial and temporal scales. In this study, the spatiotemporal characteristics of blue and green water resources (BW and GW) were evaluated based on the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), and the impacts of climate change (CC) and land-surface change (LSC) on blue-green water resources in the basin were investigated. New hydrological insights for the region First, from 2000 to 2020, both BW and GW showed an increasing trend with 3.61 mm/year and 4.63 mm/year, respectively. The spatial distribution of BW and GW changes is uneven. Second, CC drives the variations in blue-green water within the basin. LSC can locally reverse the dominant influence of climate change. Third, CC not only directly influences the spatiotemporal characteristics of blue-green water, but also alters their dynamic partitioning by modifying the land-surface conditions, notably through vegetation greening. Our results highlight that CC impacts water resources not only directly, but also indirectly by altering vegetation. This implies that water management policies account for these complex climate-vegetation-water feedbacks to ensure sustainability and resilience in the upper Yangtze River.

title: Diverging futures: The overriding influence of climate model generation (CMIP6 vs. CMIP5) on projected river-reservoir water quality and quantity under land-use change
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Vahid Pourbakhshali, Simin Heidari, Mohsen Nasseri, Seyed Taghi Omid Naeeni
abstract: Study region The Tajan watershed and Shahid Rajaei Dam reservoir, Northern Iran. Study focus Climate change, along with land-use and land-cover (LULC) variations, significantly impacts hydrological processes and water quality. Advancing climate science necessitates exploring how the latest CMIP6 scenarios improve impact projections compared to previous generations. This study evaluates the combined effects of climate and LULC changes on water quantity and quality within a river-reservoir system across various SSP and RCP scenarios. To establish a comprehensive framework, the methodology integrates the SWAT and CE-QUAL-W2 models, using downscaled CanESM2/CanESM5 outputs and annual LULC maps to combine CMIP phase comparison with river–reservoir modelling, thereby addressing the underexplored interplay of external factors in the receiving water body. However, downscaling constraints precluded uncertainty assessment of projections through multi-GCM ensembles. New hydrological insights for the region Results indicate a consistent temperature increase across all scenarios, despite variable precipitation trends during 2023–2043 compared with 2003–2022. Among non-aquatic land covers, shrublands are predicted to expand by 24.7%, while croplands shrink by 20.7%, marking the greatest changes between 2023 and 2043. Annual average streamflow is projected to increase by 4.3–19.2% across RCPs, whereas SSPs show mixed changes ranging from –5.9% to +4.3%. Similarly, nitrate loads increase by 3.9–15.1% across RCPs but change heterogeneously within the range of –6.5% to +1.6% across SSPs. Reservoir simulations show greater water-temperature increases under RCP pathways (8.4–9.4%) compared to SSPs (5.6–6.9%). Nitrate concentrations also rise by 1.9–8.2% under RCPs, while SSPs show variations ranging from –3.7% to +0.5%. Overall, RCPs exhibit more pronounced positive effects on water quantity but exert more severe impacts on water quality than SSPs, highlighting the need for mitigation strategies in dynamic, climate-LULC-driven systems.

title: Revealing multiple drought propagation characteristics on the basis of GNSS hydrometeorological data and precipitation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yongzhao Fan, Fengyu Xia, Xiufeng He, Xiaowei Zou, Pengfei Xia, Rong Zou, Jiaqi Shi, Ze Wang
abstract: Study region Yunnan Province. Study focus This study extends GNSS-based drought propagation analysis beyond time-lag estimation by introducing a risk-oriented framework. High-spatial-resolution ZTD-PE and GNSS-TWSC are first used to construct meteorological and hydrological drought indices, respectively. Subsequently, run theory, copula functions, and Bayesian conditional probability are integrated to quantify propagation time, triggering probability, and meteorological drought thresholds from 2012 to 2022, with GRACE and GLDAS used as complementary references to examine the added value of GNSS-derived water storage information. New hydrological insights Drought propagation across Yunnan is generally rapid, typically occurring within 1–6 months. Influenced by regional runoff patterns and human activities, propagation time exhibits a clear spatial pattern, with longer durations in the south and shorter durations in the north. Under meteorological drought stress, the probability of hydrological drought being triggered is significantly higher in southwestern Yunnan than in northeastern Yunnan. This pattern is closely associated with anthropogenic influences in eastern Yunnan and precipitation variability related to the southwestern monsoon. Integrated analysis using GNSS, GRACE, and GLDAS further indicates that terrestrial water storage changes in Yunnan are particularly sensitive to severe and extreme meteorological drought, especially in the southwest, whereas near-surface water responds more strongly to moderate meteorological drought, with potential implications for vegetation growth and agricultural management.

title: Three-dimensional spatio-temporal propagation dynamics from soil moisture to vegetation droughts across different eco-geographical regions of China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuxuan Du, Tao Peng, Vijay P. Singh, Ji Liu, Xiaohua Dong, Qingxia Lin, Jiali Guo, Chao Song, Dan Yu, Gaoxu Wang
abstract: Study region China. Study focus This study investigated the propagation from soil moisture drought (SD) to vegetation drought (VD) across China during 1981–2020 using a three-dimensional (3-D) spatio-temporal clustering framework. SD and VD events were identified based on the Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI) and Standardized Vegetation Health Index (SVHI), respectively. A spatio-temporal matching algorithm was developed to pair SD and VD events, enabling a quantitative analysis of propagation characteristics (i.e., propagation time, rate, direction, distance, probability, and thresholds). The key contributors were identified using an integrated XGBoost-SHAP approach. New hydrological insights for the region This study identified 144 SD and 59 VD events, among which 24 were successfully matched as propagation events. The average propagation time from SD to VD was 3.76 months, exhibiting a distinct west-to-east gradient. The thresholds for triggering VD increased with drought severity, with SD duration thresholds ranging from 1 to 6 months across most regions. Regional contributors to drought propagation time varied across China: energy-related factors were primary in humid regions, precipitation (PRE) in arid zones, and temperature (TMP) and root-zone soil moisture (SMrz) in semi-arid areas. This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding multi-dimensional drought propagation and offers scientific support for drought early warning and ecological risk management in China.

title: Contrasting effects of flash and slow droughts on maize yield loss and crop failure across Europe
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Xinxin Chen, Yean-UK Kim, Thomas Heckelei, Chenzhi Wang, Josef Baumert, Heidi Webber
abstract: Study region Europe, spanning diverse climatic zones from the semi-arid Mediterranean to the humid continental north, characterized by strong hydroclimatic variability and significant dependence on rainfed maize production. Study focus Agricultural drought risk in Europe is becoming increasingly complex, regional evidence remains limited on how drought onset speed translates to maize yield loss and crop failure across Europe's hydroclimatic zones. This study defines and distinguishes flash and slow droughts using the rate of decline in the Standardized Water Deficit Index and characterizes their spatiotemporal patterns across Europe from 1989 to 2018 and quantifies their effects on maize yield losses and crop failure using fixed effects and mixed effects logistic models. New hydrological insights for the region Firstly, both drought types showed significantly increasing trends across Europe, with slow droughts occurring more frequently than flash droughts. Secondly, flash drought was significantly associated with yield loss across four metrics (count: −208.05 kg ha−1; severity: −138.25 kg ha−1; cumulative severity: −4.13 kg ha−1; duration: −12.78 kg ha−1 day−1; all p < 0.001). Slow drought affected yield only through duration (−9.36 kg ha⁻¹ day⁻¹, p = 0.005). Thirdly, flash and slow drought significantly elevated crop failure odds across all drought metrics, with drought duration producing the strongest effects (flash: OR = 2.10; slow: OR = 2.30, p < 0.001) and slow drought consistently posing greater risk than flash drought across all metrics. This suggests that persistent moisture deficits remain critical for systemic production failure. These findings provide new regional hydrological insight by linking drought onset dynamics, root zone soil moisture deficits, and agricultural failure risk across Europe, underscoring the need for regionally tailored strategies to mitigate drought induced agricultural losses across Europe.

title: Assessment of spatiotemporal compound drought propagation in the Nakdong River basin, South Korea, using a multi-layer complex network
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ho-Jun Son, Jeongwoo Han, Hyun-Han Kwon, Tae-Woong Kim
abstract: Study region The Nakdong River basin (NRB), one of South Korea’s major river basins, exhibits significant spatial and temporal variability in drought propagation. Study focus Drought is a continuous disaster that evolves both temporally and spatially. This complex evolution process is defined as drought propagation. Previous studies have typically addressed the propagation mechanisms between different drought categories and the spatial dispersion of individual drought types as independent processes. To overcome these limitations, a multi-layer complex network approach was adopted to evaluate the spatiotemporal compound propagation of meteorological and hydrological droughts in the NRB. Furthermore, clustering of sub-watersheds by topological indicators was used to highlight distinct physical dynamics across different clusters. New hydrological insights into the region under study A total of 272 sub-watersheds in the NRB were classified into sources (28%) and sinks (72%) based on the propagation strength. Source watersheds were clustered as C1(high-intensity and multi-direction), C2(uni-direction), and C3(multi-direction), while the sink watersheds were grouped into C4(multi-direction), C5(uni-direction), and C6(high-intensity and uni-direction). Spatial analysis showed that watersheds in C1 were concentrated in the southeast, whereas those in C6 predominated in the northwest. This distribution underscored the need for proactive monitoring in the southeast and enhanced resilience in the vulnerable northwest. The propagation features were differentially associated with distinct topological indicators. Attenuation was significantly correlated with source out-strength, and sink entropy, lag with sink in-strength, and lengthening with source out-strength, sink in-strength and sink entropy. These associations demonstrated that the propagation features are linked to the structural role of each sub-watershed within the network, which conventional complex network or probabilistic approaches cannot detect. By quantifying spatiotemporal compound propagation from a network perspective, this study supports tailored drought management strategies including source control, impact mitigation, and proactive implementation of early warning systems.

title: Integrating remote sensing, machine learning, and stable isotopes to diagnose hydrological drivers and water sources of a semi-arid wetland under coal mining disturbance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zheng Yin, Caixia Liu, Ran Sun, Mingfang Tang, Shiqi Zhang, Meng Yuan, Ran Lv, Gang Wu
abstract: Study region The Tangsige Marsh Wetland is situated in the Yanjiga River Basin, Inner Mongolia, China, a semi-arid area under climatic pressure and coal mining disturbance. Study focus We designed an integrated framework that synergistically combines multi-decadal Landsat time-series analysis (Random Forest), XGBoost-SHAP driver attribution, and stable isotope tracers (δD, δ18O, d‐excess) with a Bayesian mixing model (MixSIAR) to diagnose hydrological drivers and water sources of the wetland. New hydrological insights Wetland area declined by 35.5% from 2000 to 2022, exhibiting four distinct stages of decline and recovery. DEM and NDVI dominate wetland distribution. Key drivers—NDVI, population density, and precipitation—exhibit nonlinear thresholds, and synchronous changes in their SHAP values correspond to the different evolutionary stages. Precipitation (47.9%) and groundwater (35.3%) are the dominant water sources, with coal mine drainage contributing 7.6% on average but reaching nearly 10% locally. A south-to-north gradient from groundwater-dominated to strongly evaporated precipitation-dominated explains the northern wetland's greater drought sensitivity. This macro-micro framework bridges long-term dynamics and process-scale hydrology, revealing that wetland evolution arises from the temporal alignment or misalignment of multiple drivers.

title: A TimeGAN-enhanced cross-attention time-frequency transformer for multi-step monthly runoff forecasting in the Huaihe river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Linhao Fang, Huimin Zuo, Mengtao Zhang, Zhao Zhang, Yifan Chen, Jianyou Zhu
abstract: Study region The upper Huaihe River Basin (HRB), China, with runoff observations from the Xincai (XC) and Zhoukou (ZK) hydrological stations. Study focus Data-driven models have shown considerable potential for runoff forecasting, yet their performance in monthly runoff prediction remains constrained by hydrological non-stationarity and limited data availability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Cross-Attention Time-Frequency Transformer (CA-TFAformer, CTF) framework that jointly exploits the trend, seasonal, and residual components obtained from Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (STL). A time-frequency attention (TFA) mechanism is developed to extract dominant temporal and frequency-domain characteristics, while a cross-attention (CA) mechanism is introduced to capture interactions among runoff components. Furthermore, a TimeGAN-based data augmentation strategy is employed to enrich training samples and improve model generalization. New hydrological insights for the region Monthly runoff dynamics in the upper HRB are jointly characterized by long-term trends, seasonal variability, and irregular fluctuations, indicating the importance of explicitly modeling the interactions among these runoff components. Results indicate that incorporating both time-frequency information and inter-component dependencies substantially improves forecasting performance. In addition, TimeGAN-generated samples provide additional representation of high-flow conditions in the augmented training set, resulting in more robust forecasting and improved flood peak prediction. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating runoff component interactions and data augmentation for reliable medium- and long-term runoff forecasting in non-stationary hydrological environments.

title: Enhanced total phosphorus prediction and explanation for the Minjiang upper reaches using bidirectional long short-term memory, attention mechanism, and particle swarm optimization
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Rongwen Yao, Rongsen Kong, Yungang Wu, Xiaojun Xu, Chengkang Jin, Shiwen Dai, Fuquan Yin, Zhan Xie, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yunhui Zhang
abstract: Study region Minjiang River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, China. Study focus Total phosphorus (TP) is a key contributor to water eutrophication, necessitating accurate forecasting for effective control and management. This study addresses the challenge by developing and evaluating the PSO-BiLSTM-Attn (Particle Swarm Optimization - Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory - Attention) framework for high-frequency TP prediction in the Minjiang River basin. The proposed framework is benchmarked against BP, LSTM, Transformer, and BiLSTM-Attn models using 8-hourly data from three monitoring stations across multiple forecast horizons. This study then further investigates how prediction performance varies across stations with different TP fluctuation regimes and applies explainability analysis to identify dominant drivers of TP prediction. New hydrological insights for the region Performance analysis displayed that PSO-BiLSTM-Attn achieved superior TP-level prediction compared with the baseline model, with R2 values of 0.8963 (station S1), 0.9412 (station S2), and 0.9138 (station S3). Stations with larger TP variability exhibited lower predictive performance, indicating that disturbances or stronger anthropogenic perturbations reduce model predictability. In the prediction step, single-step predictions achieved optimal accuracy for TP concentration, suggesting that TP dynamics were dominated by short-term memory and rapidly changing external inputs. The explainability analysis further indicates that TP predictions correlated positively with TN and EC, reflecting synergistic nutrient co-accumulation and pollutant-driven TP elevation, respectively. These findings provide insight into how TP dynamics respond to spatial heterogeneity and short-term disturbances in human-impacted river systems.

title: Ablation-season dynamics of a temperate glacier in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau revealed by monthly UAV surveys
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Kunpeng Wu, Yunpeng Duan, Daoxun Gao, Danyu Ma, Zhaoqi Ji, Francesca Baldacchino, Tobias Bolch, Shiyin Liu, Cheng Huang
abstract: Study region Yanong Glacier is a large lake-terminating temperate glacier in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, a hydrologically important region influenced by the Indian monsoon. Study focus This study investigates ablation-season glacier dynamics using six UAV surveys conducted over the glacier tongue from June to November 2023. High-resolution DSMs and DOMs were used to quantify elevation change and surface velocity, and to evaluate the links among ice-flow resupply, surface lowering, and velocity variability. New hydrological insights for the region The glacier tongue thinned by 3.43 ± 0.03 m and showed an average horizontal displacement of 0.412 ± 0.001 m d−1 during the ablation season. In the moraine-bounded section, ice-flow resupply partly compensated surface melt, with sensitivity bounds of approximately 14–26% under ±30% ice-thickness perturbations. Short-term velocity variability could not be explained by thickness- and slope-driven internal deformation alone; instead, a substantial residual basal-motion component remained. The covariation among air temperature, surface lowering, and residual basal motion suggests a plausible melt-velocity linkage, but does not provide direct proof of basal-sliding control. These monthly UAV observations help constrain the timing of meltwater production, lake-terminus dynamics, and seasonal glacier-related hazards in this data-scarce region.

title: Differences in water retention performance among multiple water storage media in the karst epikarst under drying-wetting alternation events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haijun Ma, Yuan Li, Qiuwen Zhou, Xukun Zheng
abstract: Study region A typical subtropical karst epikarst in southwestern China. Study focus Global climate change has intensified drying-wetting alternation, posing a severe challenge to the water storage capacity of karst regions. This study aims to establish an integrated observation system for different water storage media in a typical karst epikarst, using eight drying-wetting alternation events (DWAE) to quantitatively compare their water retention performance and elucidate hydrological response mechanisms. New hydrological insight The four water storage media in the karst epikarst show a clear gradient in water retention performance: deep fissure soil (120–240 cm) has the highest water content (32.2 ± 3.1%) and the lowest CV (9.5%), demonstrating the best retention; shallow fissure soil (0–120 cm) ranks second (27.1 ± 2.9%, CV 11.1%); topsoil, limited by evapotranspiration and storage capacity, shows greater fluctuations (15.9%-30.4%, CV 16.5%) and relatively weak retention; rock fissures, with limited storage space but high connectivity, exhibit the most dramatic water content variations (rainy season CV 43.8%, dry season CV 28.2%) and the weakest retention (5.1%-24.3%), serving mainly as rapid transport and temporary storage pathways. The study also reveals that, during drying-wetting alternation events, these media exhibit delayed vertical recharge and preferential shallow release. These findings deepen understanding of water regulation in the karst epikarst, providing a scientific basis for water resource management and ecological restoration under karst habitats.

title: Modeling flow persistence in headwater basins using climatic and morphometric data and machine learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Tony Vinicius Moreira Sampaio, Jorge Rocha, Cláudia Morais Viana, Fábio Marcelo Breunig, Elias Fernando Berra, Elaine de Cacia de Lima Frick, Edenilson Roberto do Nascimento
abstract: Study Region Southern Brazil, specifically the state of Paraná, characterized by distinct geomorphological units and subtropical to temperate climatic conditions. Study Focus This study investigates the controls of flow persistence (perennial vs. intermittent conditions) in first-order headwater basins using climatic and morphometric variables within a machine-learning framework. Rather than focusing on the hydrogeological origin of springs, the analysis targets the surface expression of flow regimes in headwater channels. A Random Forest (RF) classifier was applied to 164 basins with field-verified flow conditions using 152 predictors derived from ERA5-Land reanalysis and terrain metrics, including the Roughness Concentration Index (RCI). Model performance was evaluated through 1000 iterations and 10-fold cross-validation and optimized through systematic variable reduction to identify a parsimonious and physically interpretable set of predictors. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Results show that local morphometric properties, particularly terrain roughness (RCI), combined with hydroclimatic variables (runoff, precipitation, and vegetation indices), exert stronger control on flow persistence than basin area alone. The RF model achieved 78.2% accuracy (AUC = 0.84), outperforming traditional mapping approaches, while maintaining stable performance with only eight variables. These findings indicate that flow persistence in subtropical headwaters emerges from nonlinear interactions between terrain structure and climatic forcing, providing a scalable framework for hydrological assessment and water-resource management in data-scarce regions.

title: Luís Ribeiro: A visionary mind bridging groundwater science, culture and music through an interdisciplinary and humanistic legacy
How density and viscosity differences cause nonuniform flow distribution across well screens and impact heat recovery of HT-ATES systems
abstract: Abstract It is well known that heat recovery of high-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) systems is negatively impacted by buoyancy-driven flow of the injected hot, low-density water during storage. Density differences, however, also affect pressure head conditions within the well and therefore pressure head differences with the aquifer. Thus, it was anticipated that nonuniform flow distribution across the well screen may occur even when homogeneous aquifer permeability is assumed. In this study, the extent and conditions under which nonuniform flow across HT-ATES well screens occurs, influenced by both variable density and viscosity, were evaluated using both numerical and analytical approaches. Results show that with larger density differences (injection temperatures up to 90 °C) and lower well pressure heads, flow distribution is increasingly nonuniform, with the highest flow rates across the top part of the well screen, up to multiple times the average flow rate. Nonuniformity is described analytically by the maximum depth of injection ( D inj,max ) and the maximum normalized flow at the top of the aquifer ( q n,max ). Decreasing viscosities with higher temperatures further amplify buoyancy-induced nonuniform flow distribution, with flow rates up to 3.7 times the average. Flow distribution is shown to be asymmetrical during injection and extraction, and besides contributing to losses, the extent to which flow distribution is nonuniform, consequently also results in substantially higher maximum velocities across the borehole wall, which is a critical design parameter to prevent clogging. A literature screening of HT-ATES storage conditions in practice highlights the relevance of considering buoyancy-induced nonuniform flow distribution.

title: Calibration of a 3D regional groundwater model using geophysics-derived groundwater levels
Salinization and freshening by extracting fresh and brackish groundwater from transition zones: Insights from a field study in the Dutch coastal dunes and implications for freshwater extractability
abstract: Abstract Extracting brackish groundwater using scavenger wells beneath freshwater lenses can mitigate salinization of freshwater wells. However, disturbing the fresh–saline transition zone may induce losses from limited freshwater reserves through mixing and groundwater quality changes. A field study was conducted in the Dutch coastal dunes that combines geophysical and hydrogeochemical analyses to examine disturbances from well installation, salinity dynamics during fresh and brackish groundwater extraction, and mixing and ion-exchange processes affecting extracted groundwater quality. Fresh drilling fluid introduced during well installation primarily freshened deeper, more saline groundwater. Residual drilling fluid persisted mainly in clay seals after well development, affecting geophysical measurements. Nevertheless, applying fresh drilling fluid and clay seals improved long-term representativeness of groundwater quality monitoring by limiting ion exchange and vertical mixing within the borehole. Extracting brackish groundwater in addition to freshwater nearly tripled the 4-month freshwater extractability (from 48,000 to 142,000 m 3 ) at the pilot site, with limited losses owing to freshwater mixing in the brackish scavenger well (19,000 m 3 ). Alternatively, when extracting brackish groundwater only, the local expansion of the freshwater lens was limited relative to the estimated losses by mixing in the brackish well. Freshwater extraction triggered salinization-induced mobilization of freshwater cations (ammonium, barium, calcium, iron, and manganese). Concurrent brackish groundwater extraction stabilized extracted freshwater quality, but instead triggered ion exchange in extracted brackish groundwater. Overall, this study identifies freshwater losses and water quality changes as key design constraints for optimizing scavenger well installation and operation, aiming to increase coastal freshwater extractability.

title: Interactive educational applications for hydrogeology and groundwater management
abstract: Abstract Groundwater, which constitutes a significant share of the globally available freshwater, is a resource that receives little public attention because of its hidden nature. In university education, hydrogeology or groundwater hydrology is typically included in geology, environmental, or engineering courses, but often receives little emphasis. The study of hydrogeology and groundwater management is challenging because to fully understand the topic, a large variety of competencies are required, ranging from applied field and laboratory methods to quantitative analysis that involves advanced mathematical, physical, and chemical concepts. These challenges call for educational approaches that make the complex and abstract subsurface processes more accessible and transparent. This article provides an overview of recent advances in interactive educational applications based primarily on the Python programming language embedded in HTML/CSS or JavaScript. It introduces existing frameworks for developing and utilizing these applications, offering educators and students tools to enhance learning experiences in hydrogeology and groundwater management. The paper explores uses for interactive applications, including classroom settings, self-directed learning, and continuing education. Practical examples of these educational tools are presented alongside detailed instructions for their implementation, enabling educators to integrate these open-source resources into their teaching practice effectively as well as to advance the tools.

title: Groundwater exploration in typical geomorphological settings of the karst region of southwest China
Correction: Regional and local controls on groundwater salinity in California’s southwestern San Joaquin Valley, United States: Insights from airborne electromagnetic surveys
Numerical simulation of coupled chemical dissolution and nonlinear seepage in a single carbonate-rock fracture
Socio-hydrogeology: The past, present, and future of a people-centred and place-based approach to groundwater science
abstract: Groundwater systems are shaped by deeply interwoven physical processes and social dynamics, yet traditional hydrogeological approaches have often treated these domains separately. Over the past decade, socio-hydrogeology has emerged in response, offering an approach that systematically incorporates social dimensions into hydrogeological investigations. In its initial formulation, socio-hydrogeology was meant to raise awareness among hydrogeologists of the social implications of their work, fostering engagement with water users and interdisciplinary collaboration from the onset of research. Since then, the approach has gained academic traction and institutional recognition, yet it still lacks a clear conceptual definition, posing risks to its coherence and impact. This paper marks 10 years since the term’s inception and critically reflects on the development and future direction of socio-hydrogeology. By critically analysing the evolution of the concept and situating it among broader inter- and transdisciplinary frameworks, this paper proposes an updated conceptualisation to clarify its disciplinary scope, practical relevance, and further encourage its application. Attention is also given to the implications for hydrogeological education, arguing for a shift in pedagogy that better equips researchers to engage with the ethical and cultural dimensions of groundwater science. Socio-hydrogeology offers an opportunity to reframe hydrogeology not only as a natural science but as one deeply shaped by (and accountable to) society.

title: General or specialized programmes in hydrogeology? Insights from long-term experience in Serbia
An adaptive multifidelity surrogates-based data assimilation approach for groundwater contamination sources identification
Isotopic investigations on identification of atmospheric moisture origins and evaluation of runoff source contributions to the Upper Beas River Basin in the western Himalayas
Exploring the benefits of industry and community engagement in hydrogeology teaching
abstract: Abstract The role of industry engagement in hydrogeology education remains undervalued, despite its potential to enhance student learning and career readiness. Integrating both industry and community partnerships can increase student engagement, deepen students understanding of hydrogeological concepts and raise awareness of career opportunities, potentially improving graduate outcomes. This study evaluates the integration of such partnerships in the “Groundwater Systems” unit at the Queensland University of Technology (QUT), Brisbane, Australia. The approach involved collaborating with industry partners, revising assessment and progressively expanding opportunities for student–industry engagement. Surveys were conducted to evaluate the success of this engagement and to identify barriers limiting student participation. The groundwater unit now features semester-long industry interactions, including immersion in community-linked groundwater research projects as part of major assessments. The observed benefits of this include increased interest in the subject material and enhanced understanding of hydrogeology concepts and methods. Alumni participation as industry guest speakers further demonstrates the potential for sustained partnerships to enhance graduate outcomes.

title: Groundwater–surface water interactions and resilience to hydrological extremes in a data-sparse arid transboundary river basin: Insights from collaborative groundwater modelling
abstract: Abstract Sustainable groundwater management is key to building resilience to hydrological extremes but remains challenging in data-scarce transboundary river basins. In this study, a transboundary, collaborative, physically based groundwater modelling approach has been developed for the Limpopo River Basin (LRB), which is highly vulnerable to floods and droughts. Monitoring data and model results consistently suggest that prolonged wet periods and floods significantly raised groundwater levels, whereas prolonged droughts decreased them, particularly in the upstream and central regions of the basin characterized by low-storage fractured bedrock aquifers. Groundwater–surface water interactions are greater downstream, where water tables are shallower in unconsolidated superficial materials, and intensify during floods, especially in the central region. Modelling results also suggest that baseflow is less responsive to extremes than groundwater recharge across the LRB, highlighting the groundwater system’s attenuation capacity. The model was subsequently used to assess and discuss a series of co-created management scenarios focused specifically on improving groundwater storage during wet periods for use during dry periods. They included: (1) managed aquifer recharge (MAR), using (1a) injection well(s) next to large dams, (1b) rainwater and runoff harvesting (RRH) and infiltration through local wells, (1c) RRH through local ponds and (1d) small reservoirs (e.g. sand dams); (2) deforestation; (3) afforestation; and (4) increased groundwater abstraction. Scenarios suggest that strategy (1b), when widely applied across the basin, may be the most effective to reduce the risk and impact of floods, droughts, and groundwater depletion by supporting the maintenance of groundwater levels and baseflow, while reducing storm runoff.

title: A climate change perspective on groundwater vulnerability assessment using a static and non-static variable approach: A regional multi-aquifer case study
Geological and hydrogeological functioning of aquifers in the Gareb Plain, northeastern Morocco: Insights from exploratory drilling and seismic reflection imaging
Correction: Hydrogeological modeling and global climate change impacts on the last permanent sand-dune pond in the Doñana World Heritage Site: Santa Olalla Pond, Spain
Mechanistic insights into heterogeneous saturated–unsaturated seepage dynamics: A paradigm-shifting 3D framework for dam stability analysis
Lithological schematization of the Karnali fluvial fan (Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape) using electrical resistivity tomography as a basis for hydrogeological investigations
abstract: Abstract In the Nepalese and Indian Terai Arc Landscape (TAL), protected nature areas are supported by groundwater systems that have remained largely understudied. This study schematizes the lithology of the Karnali fluvial fan located in the Bardia district (Nepal) as a basis for future hydrogeological investigations. Inversion results of 2D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) profiles at 21 locations were interpreted by comparing with the local borehole lithology and regional geophysical studies. Multiple lithological cross-sections were prepared to develop a 3D lithological model spanning the fan, and the adjacent Bardia National Park up to the Babai River in the east. Sediment resistivities found were in the range of 8–6000 Ω m. Resistivity less than 40 Ω m was identified as clay, 40–80 Ω m represented silt and fine sand, 80–400 Ω m identified as fine to coarse sand and resistivities higher than 400 Ω m were interpreted as coarse sand, gravel and boulders. A coarse sand-gravelly layer is present at the fan apex and along the foot of the Himalayas in the north that functions as a recharge area and aquifer. The central part of the fan has sandy layers which transition to fine sand and silt layers in the distal south and southeast. Clay layers locally create confining conditions, within the sand and silt dominated areas. These findings on subsurface lithology provide valuable insights for the groundwater systems which sustain ecohydrological processes relevant to the protected ecosystem and fills a critical knowledge gap on regional hydrogeology of the TAL.

title: Response mechanisms of surrounding rock and tunnel structures of a karst tunnel under high operational water pressure
Correction: A geological and geophysical database for the assessment of offshore freshened groundwater resources
Determining hydraulic conductivity and porosity sensitivity of grain-size analysis methods using laboratory and small-scale model measurements
abstract: Abstract Hydraulic conductivity (K) is essential for determining seepage flow in porous media. In this study, a small-scale model (SSM) was tested using coarse sand (CS) and medium sand (MS) samples, designed according to the similarity model law. In the SSM, pumping tests were carried out in laboratory conditions to estimate K . This technique combines the advantages of field and laboratory measurements. The results of SSM measurements were validated by a constant head permeameter. Employing the validated SSM-based K values, 31 grain-size analysis methods (GSAMs) were compared and evaluated. For both soil samples, the US Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) method provided the best results. Sensitivity analysis for porosity was performed on 17 GSAMs using four theoretical and two laboratory methods. It was concluded that laboratory-based porosity measurements are recommended to obtain more accurate K values. Of the theoretical methods, Wooster gave the smallest relative difference for CS, whereas the Wu and Wang method performed best for MS. Considering the GSAMs, the Arshad, Carrier, Chapuis, Chapuis and Aubertin, Fair and Hatch, Kozeny-Carman, Mbonimpa, Pavchich, Sauerbrei, and Shahabi methods were found to be very sensitive to porosity, while the Kasenow and Koenders, and Williams methods are the least sensitive. For five GSAMs, the possibility arises that an added constant can be used to improve the calculated K values which was demonstrated in this study through a recommendation for the Kasenow constant.

title: A GIS-based multi-criteria and evolutionary optimization framework for groundwater monitoring network design and well selection
Using pumping tests to understand how sea proximity and karstification influence the hydraulics of a coastal karstic aquifer in the Yucatan Peninsula
Mechanisms of groundwater circulation driven by coal mining in arid western China: Hydrogeochemical and stable isotope evidence
Technical design and hydrogeochemical evaluation of a stormwater-based managed aquifer recharge pilot site in an intensively cultivated region (Hallertau, Germany)
abstract: Abstract Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) with stormwater remains underexplored in rural settings due to uncertainties related to source-water variability, treatment performance, and groundwater-quality impacts. This study presents the design and hydrogeochemical evaluation of a stormwater-based MAR pilot site implemented in 2024 in Hüll (Bavaria, Germany), a flood-prone agricultural region underlain by a heterogeneous Tertiary aquifer. The system integrates a stormwater retention basin, treatment units, an infiltration well, and a comprehensive monitoring framework combining multi-parameter online sensors, detailed laboratory analyses, and contextual information on catchment activities. Hydraulic testing confirmed strong aquifer heterogeneity but also demonstrated high injectivity of the target formation. Hydrochemical monitoring evaluated raw water characteristics, treatment efficiency, and groundwater responses. The treatment unit effectively removed pesticides and substantially reduced suspended solids, while stormwater nitrate concentrations were consistently lower than those in groundwater, indicating dilution potential during recharge. The pilot demonstrates that rural stormwater can serve as a reliable MAR source under variable hydrological conditions. The integrated design and monitoring concept provides a transferable framework for similar agricultural regions and supports future calibration of site-scale hydrogeological and reactive transport models.

title: A lumped model with vadose filtering and quadratic drainage for daily groundwater recharge estimation
abstract: Abstract Quantifying groundwater recharge at a daily temporal resolution is difficult when inputs are sparse. This research presents a simple lumped model that links precipitation to groundwater levels by (1) routing rainfall through a first-order exponential vadose filter followed by an explicit discrete delay, and (2) representing lateral drainage with a nonlinear (quadratic) outflow law. The saturated storage is tracked with specific yield ( S y ), and the model advances at a daily time step, producing time series of recharge, head, and lateral flow. The approach was tested with daily precipitation data from nearby rainfall stations and groundwater levels from four wells in the Bauru Aquifer System (BAS, Brazil). The model reproduces the timing and amplitude of observed hydraulic heads across seasonal cycles, capturing delayed and attenuated recharge pulses and curvilinear recessions, with a normalized root mean square error (RMSE) < 14% against observations. Relative to the water-table fluctuation (WTF) method, the mass balance explicitly accounts for concurrent lateral drainage during recharge events and for vadose delay/attenuation, explaining systematically higher, but process-consistent, recharge fractions than the WTF method. Parameter estimates are hydrologically interpretable, although equifinality requires validating fitted values against independent aquifer information. The method provides fast recharge diagnostics from long daily records without requiring daily evapotranspiration, making it suitable for basin-scale screening and trend attribution, and extensible to multistress forcing where data permit.

title: Comment on “Informing future management decisions by comparison of the largest freshwater spring in the southeastern Mojave Desert with groundwater quality from downgradient wells, Mojave Trails National Monument, USA”: Report published in Hydrogeology Journal (2025) 33:2181–2196, by Luke Stevens and David K. Kreamer

Reply to Comment on “Informing future management decisions by comparison of the largest freshwater spring in the southeastern Mojave Desert with groundwater quality from downgradient wells, Mojave Trails National Monument, USA”: Report published in Hydrogeology Journal (2025) 33:2181–2196, by Luke J. Stevens and David K. Kreamer
Assessing groundwater potential and recharge zones in the headwaters of the Blue Nile River, Ethiopia
Impact of changing rainfall patterns on groundwater recharge in semi-arid dune landscapes
abstract: Abstract Climate-induced changes in rainfall patterns, particularly increases in event intensity and altered seasonal distribution, pose significant challenges for groundwater recharge and water resource management, especially in semi-arid Mediterranean environments. This study was motivated by the pronounced scarcity of long-term field data quantifying how rainfall intensity and vegetation cover interact to shape the soil water budget and diffuse recharge under natural conditions. To address this gap, a 3-year lysimeter experiment was conducted in the aeolian dune system of Doñana National Park (SW Spain), utilizing four precision weighable lysimeters of different sizes and vegetation covers (bare soil, pine canopy, and shrubland). Meteorological and hydrological variables were continuously monitored, allowing detailed partitioning of precipitation, evaporation, and drainage at high temporal resolution. The results show that a small number of high-intensity storms (> 20 mm/day) dominated annual rainfall input and were responsible for most groundwater recharge, whereas low-intensity rainfall contributed negligibly to recharge. Bare-soil lysimeters exhibited consistently high and stable recharge rates (50–55% of rainfall), while vegetated lysimeters showed much lower and more variable recharge (11–60%), with intense storms effectively bypassing interception and transpiration limits. These findings illustrate that vegetation cover critically modulates the effect of rainfall intensity on recharge, with groundwater input under vegetation potentially matching bare soil recharge when intense events are frequent. This insight has important implications for understanding and managing groundwater resources in sandy, semi-arid regions undergoing climate-driven changes in rainfall regime.

title: Revisiting the hydrogeological water balance of Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain): Implications for sustainable groundwater exploitation
abstract: Abstract Balancing groundwater exploitation with ecological preservation requires robust conceptual models, particularly in karst systems where aquifer–lake interactions are complex and highly sensitive to human and climatic pressures. Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain) is a groundwater-fed karstic-tectonic system of exceptional ecological value, yet its hydrogeological functioning remains insufficiently understood. This study revisits its water balance by integrating meteorological, limnological, hydrochemical, and isotopic data into an updated hydrogeological analysis. Results indicate that regional groundwater inflow from the Banyoles–Alta Garrotxa system contributes ~11.4 × 10 6 m 3 /year, equivalent to ~54% of total inputs to the lake, while local recharge through runoff and shallow aquifers represents only ~23%. Outflows are dominated by drains (~16.2 × 10 6 m 3 /year, 77% of total) and evaporation (~2.3 × 10 6 m 3 /year 11%). The refined conceptual model highlights the predominance of upward vertical flows from confined limestone aquifers through a karstified gypsum formation, which govern lake recharge and explain the observed sulphate enrichment of lake water. This framework challenges conventional interpretations that treat the lake surface as a constant-head boundary, instead recognizing it as a dynamic hydrogeological unit controlled by potentiometric head of the aquifer beneath, which has seldom been addressed in the hydrogeological literature. By clarifying the processes sustaining Banyoles Lake hydrogeology, this report provides a novel conceptual framework essential for sustainable groundwater governance under increasing climatic stress.

title: Water–rock interaction controls on hydrogeochemical evolution of alluvial groundwater in high-altitude alpine regions of China
Collaborative learning: the school of hydrogeological modelling and project-related strategies (SYMPLE) community experience
Correction: Earthquake correction enabled holistic assessment of water storage variations in Japan
Evaluating the interaction between karst and evaporite formations to identify the origin and mechanism of groundwater salinization
Participatory groundwater management in peri-urban areas with informal water markets: Insights from a socio-hydrogeological case study in Jaipur, India
abstract: Abstract In many peri-urban areas of the Global South, formal water supply systems are insufficient. This gap is largely filled by a diverse informal water market and widespread informal water use, both of which depend heavily on groundwater. Peri-urban low-income communities are particularly affected. Research in such contexts requires participatory and interdisciplinary approaches. This paper aims to equip hydrogeologists with the knowledge needed to implement participatory management, thereby fostering deeper engagement with participatory methodologies and strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration. The findings are also intended to support NGOs in planning more comprehensive water projects by integrating hydrogeological considerations. Two low-income communities in peri-urban Jaipur, India, representing different hydrogeological, infrastructural, and socio-cultural conditions, were selected as study areas in cooperation with a local NGO. The study comprised four components: initial socio-hydrogeological assessments to gain baseline information; water workshops to raise awareness and exchange knowledge on groundwater; the recruitment and training of women assistants to teach a small group more advanced groundwater-related skills; and finally, the production of films to disseminate the results. The research demonstrated that the applied methods generated relevant insights and enabled the implementation of a participatory approach. However, future studies should engage more thoroughly with the literature on participatory methodologies, ideally in collaboration with social scientists experienced in such approaches. Despite these limitations, the study contributes to the growing field of participatory and socio-hydrogeological research and shows that these approaches can enhance groundwater awareness among local communities and NGOs while sensitizing hydrogeologists to the importance of inter- and transdisciplinary work.

title: Educating for groundwater sustainability in a changing world: A joint, applied, interdisciplinary and inclusive postgraduate approach
abstract: Abstract Safeguarding groundwater, a vital resource in adaptation to global change, yet increasingly under pressure, requires robust knowledge and capacity. While strong foundations in hydrogeology remain indispensable, there is a clear need for joint, interdisciplinary and applied groundwater education at the postgraduate level to address the complex and multifaceted nature of groundwater science. Building on these arguments, the Joint Master’s Programme Groundwater and Global Change was successfully launched a decade ago. This essay presents the rationale behind this approach.

title: 25 years of PEST courses: A few reflections
Hydrogeology education in Germany: Did things develop since 2001?
abstract: Abstract The essay describes the development of hydrogeology education in German universities over the past 25 years, based on the author’s own experience and an informal poll among German-speaking hydrogeology lecturers. Hydrogeology is an integral part of geoscience degree programmes in Germany, where it is increasingly recognized as an indispensable player in interdisciplinary efforts to solve societal, environmental and health-related problems. This is reflected by faculty positions in Germany shifting towards a focus on (bio) geochemistry and away from groundwater quantity-focused research.

title: Reflections on hydrogeology education and lifelong learning
abstract: Abstract There is a strong global demand for hydrogeological expertise, yet educational opportunities for hydrogeologists are not so widely available. Taught masters programmes can provide hydrogeologists with the fundamentals of groundwater science and many of its wider applications. Groundwater engineering (including well design, construction and pumping systems) should feature more strongly in such hydrogeology courses. Scientific associations such as the International Association of Hydrogeologists (IAH) can make a significant contribution to lifelong learning through training courses, mentoring and educational materials.

title: Divergent transport behaviors of fluorescent nanoparticles versus sodium fluorescein in fractured media
The use of pumping for hydraulic characterisation of dykes
abstract: Abstract Faults and dykes can control groundwater flow, acting as barriers, conduits, or composite conduit–barrier systems. This study investigates dyke hydraulic behaviour using numerical modelling of field-scale pumping tests at two sites in Western Australia, supported by a uniquely detailed hydrogeological dataset. At each site, pumping tests were conducted across dykes that impeded groundwater flow, as evidenced by asymmetric drawdown cones and delayed responses in observation wells situated across the dyke from the pumping well. High-resolution three-dimensional geological frameworks were developed, and transient groundwater flow models were calibrated using automated inversion with and without spatially variable parameterisation (pilot points) to represent heterogeneity. In all calibrated models, the horizontal hydraulic conductivity ( K h ) of dykes was estimated to be one to eight orders of magnitude lower than that of the surrounding formations. Representation of dykes in the model produced the largest improvement in model fit at both sites, reducing the parameterisation objective function by one to two orders of magnitude relative to model parameterisations without dykes. Further improvements in model fit were achieved by introducing heterogeneity into formations, dykes or both. Although including formation heterogeneity reduced posterior uncertainty in dyke K h estimates, posterior variance patterns revealed that, in some locations, calibration preferentially adjusted K h in formations adjacent to dykes rather than within the dykes. Dyke K h was tightly constrained in areas with available field data and observable drawdown. These findings demonstrate the importance of representing structural features when interpreting pumping-test responses in structurally complex groundwater systems.

title: A simulation-surrogate-optimization model for inversion of groundwater contamination source characteristics in fractured aquifers
Unveiling aquifer architecture and qualitative potential in the lower Choapa River basin, semiarid Chile
Characterizing groundwater flow using an acoustic Doppler current profiler in sinkholes of the Yucatán Península, Mexico
Radon (222Rn) activation processes in shallow aquifers in fractured crystalline rocks: A model constrained by long-term monitoring and tracer tests
abstract: Abstract Sixteen years of monitoring at St. Vojtěch Springs (Giant Mountains, Czech Republic) form the basis for a calibrated model explaining variations in 222 Rn activity in crystalline aquifers. The model enables estimation of activation zone length (fractures rich in parent radioisotopes) and saturated 222 Rn activity. Eleven springs with an activation zone of primary uranium mineralization in orthogneiss at the contact with dolomite have 222 Rn activities in the range of 185–5469 Bq L −1 , which varies with flow rate. The objective of this study was to quantify the relationship between flow velocity and 222 Rn activity using tracer data and long-term observations. An exponential mathematical model was calibrated at one of the springs with an average flow velocity of 0.44 m h −1 , the saturated 222 Rn activity was 5160 Bq L −1 , and the length of the activation zone was 44 m; these parameters determine 222 Rn activity at each flow rate point. Subsequently, the model was expanded to include various lengths of activation zones and decay zones in which 222 Rn activity decreases due to missing parent isotopes. In fractured, crystalline bedrock aquifers where 222 Rn activity and flow rate relationships are established across various flow conditions, this model provides robust analytical capabilities. With sufficient monitoring data, the lengths of both the activation and the decay zone can be estimated. Without tracer tests, the model can still be applied, estimating the effective pore volumes of both zones instead of their lengths. This research advances the fundamental understanding of radon transport mechanisms in fractured crystalline bedrock aquifer systems.

title: Hydrochemical and sedimentary effects on hydrogeological properties following mine-water reinjection into low-permeability sandstone aquifers
Revealing the hydrological cycle of karst water in Southwestern China’s subterranean river basins from the perspective of hydrogen and oxygen isotopes
Integrated conceptual–numerical modeling of high-flux groundwater seepage during deep excavation on coastal reclaimed land
abstract: Abstract High-flux groundwater seepage occurred during deep excavation at a landfill construction site on coastal reclaimed land in South Korea. In this study, the cause of the groundwater seepage was analyzed using integrated conceptual and numerical modeling techniques. Ten candidate hydrogeological conceptual models (HCMs) were developed by combining various configurations of subsurface hydrogeological units (HGUs) and different magnitudes of the seepage phenomenon. Numerical groundwater models, based on these HCMs, were built using a three-dimensional stratigraphic model derived from borehole data to simulate the distribution of HGUs and groundwater seepage. Among the numerical models, the one that best reproduced the observed water levels, seepage, and drawdown was selected and further refined through model calibration. The final HCM provided insights into the site’s hydrogeological system and enabled a forensic interpretation of the groundwater seepage mechanism. The high-flux groundwater discharge was attributed to a groundwater upwelling phenomenon that hydraulically connects deep permeable media to the excavation surface. Weathered bedrock located approximately 22 m below the ground surface were found to be sufficiently permeable to serve as a source layer for the seepage. Through case studies of additional excavation and drainage strategies, the integrated conceptual–numerical modeling approach demonstrated its potential as a reliable predictive tool for designing response strategies to groundwater seepage. This approach also facilitates interdisciplinary communication and supports adaptive site management throughout the project lifecycle, highlighting its practical engineering relevance.

title: Comparative analysis of lineament mapping using Sentinel-1A, Landsat 8 OLI, and ALOS PALSAR for hydrogeological applications in the Moroccan Central Massif
Groundwater-based water services as complex socio-hydrogeological systems: insights from Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
abstract: Abstract Groundwater systems are critical to global water security, yet the complex interactions between household coping strategies, resource sustainability, and climate change remain difficult to govern. This study applies qualitative systems mapping to characterise socio-hydrogeological dynamics in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta, a region currently facing intensifying saline intrusion and rapid land-use change. Drawing on a household survey ( n = 404) and in-depth interviews ( n = 25) in Sóc Trăng and Trà Vinh provinces, three critical system interactions were identified: (1) climate variability and household adaptation intensify groundwater system pressures, (2) policy-practice gaps undermine effective management of a multisource water system, and (3) social vulnerability and water stress constrain resilience. Together, these interactions illustrate how household behaviours, institutional arrangements, and resource conditions are interconnected in ways that shape system behaviour. These findings advance socio-hydrogeological frameworks by using systems mapping to make visible the relationships and interactions that influence groundwater-based water services. The research offers evidence for policymakers, suggesting that inclusive, climate-resilient service delivery depends on integrating actual household water behaviours into planning and groundwater governance, moving beyond a singular focus on piped supply.

title: Risk assessment of tunnelling-induced hydrogeological interference on springs using a machine learning approach
abstract: Abstract Tunnel excavation through mountain ranges can alter groundwater regimes, affecting spring discharge and dependent ecosystems. Anticipating these interferences is essential for environmental risk management, cost–benefit analysis, and effective mitigation planning. Conventional assessment methods are largely parametric, not physically based, and heavily dependent on expert judgment, introducing subjectivity and uncertainty. This study proposes a data-driven approach based on machine learning (ML), specifically a Random Forest (RF) model, to evaluate hydrogeological risk and spring vulnerability during the preliminary design phase of tunnels. The method exploits geological information typically available in early stages and is validated using two well-documented Italian case studies: The Bologna–Florence high-speed railway line, excavated in fractured sedimentary formations of the Northern Apennines, and the Gran Sasso highway tunnels, driven in karstified carbonate rocks of the Central Apennines. Both datasets are published, hydrogeologically validated, and supported by detailed pre- and post-excavation monitoring, ensuring robustness and consistency. The ML framework demonstrates strong predictive performance across standard classification metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the curve (AUC). While it employs input parameters comparable to those of parametric methods such as the drawdown hazard index (DHI), it differs by deriving parameter weights directly from data. Moreover, the use of Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values enhances interpretability, mitigates black-box behaviour, and allows expert knowledge to be effectively integrated. The innovation, therefore, lies in offering a transferable and reproducible tool to support early-stage tunnelling decisions, representing a clear improvement over traditional qualitative or semi-quantitative approaches.
